#!/bin/bash
# eg-q — FAIR wrapper over the AUDIT-PATCHED eg-q.orig.
#
# MEASURED PROBLEM (logs/tofix.py, 101 eg sessions):
#   The first payload already names a gold file in 77% of sessions (68/88). When it does, the agent
#   still makes 6.59 MORE calls before touching that file (n=39). The dominant shapes are
#   `eg:search -> eg:def -> eg:grep` and `eg:search -> eg:grep -> eg:grep`: three graph calls to
#   settle ONE location. And logs/tofind.py: eg reaches gold in 4.77 calls vs grep's 3.62 -- the tool
#   is 1.15 calls SLOWER at the one job it exists for.
#
# WHY the agent re-asks: the top hit's body is a MEDIAN 357 B (mean 994 B) -- a fragment, not a
# symbol. It cannot be edited against, so `def` follows immediately. The fix is to make `search`
# TERMINAL: fold the full definition in when the printed body is short, so there is nothing left to
# verify. This is a completeness change, not a width change.
#
# FAIRNESS: tool output only. No sentence a no-tool arm could act on. No imperative, no turn budget,
# no verify command. Bytes are capped and the fold is SKIPPED when the body is already complete.
#
# REVERT: cp tools/eg-q.pre-deffold tools/eg-q
set -uo pipefail
EGQ="${EGQ_REAL:-$(dirname "$0")/eg-q.orig}"
EG_FOLD_IMPACT="${EG_FOLD_IMPACT:-1}"
EG_FOLD_IMPACT_MAXB="${EG_FOLD_IMPACT_MAXB:-3000}"
EG_FOLD_DEF="${EG_FOLD_DEF:-1}"
EG_FOLD_DEF_MINB="${EG_FOLD_DEF_MINB:-700}"    # fold only if hit-1 body is smaller than this
EG_FOLD_DEF_MAXB="${EG_FOLD_DEF_MAXB:-2600}"

_hit1_sym() { sed -n 's/^[[:space:]]*1\..*[[:space:]]symbol=\([^[:space:]]*\).*/\1/p' | head -1; }

_body1_bytes() {   # bytes of hit 1's printed body: lines after the "1." header until the next "N."
  awk 'BEGIN{inb=0;n=0}
       /^[[:space:]]*1\.[[:space:]]/{inb=1;next}
       /^[[:space:]]*[0-9]+\.[[:space:]]/{if(inb){exit}}
       { if(inb){n+=length($0)+1} }
       END{print n+0}'
}

_fold() {   # stdin = search output; echo it, then append def (if body is thin) and impact
  local out; out="$(cat)"
  printf '%s\n' "$out"
  local sym; sym="$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | _hit1_sym)"
  [ -n "$sym" ] || return 0

  if [ "$EG_FOLD_DEF" = 1 ]; then
    local b; b="$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | _body1_bytes)"
    if [ "${b:-0}" -lt "$EG_FOLD_DEF_MINB" ] 2>/dev/null; then
      local dfn; dfn="$("$EGQ" def "$sym" 2>/dev/null || true)"
      if [ -n "$dfn" ] && [ "${#dfn}" -le "$EG_FOLD_DEF_MAXB" ]; then
        printf '\nFULL DEFINITION OF %s (complete symbol at real line numbers; the body above was a\nfragment, so this is the text to edit against):\n%s\n' "$sym" "$dfn"
      fi
    fi
  fi

  if [ "$EG_FOLD_IMPACT" = 1 ]; then
    local imp; imp="$("$EGQ" impact "$sym" 2>/dev/null || true)"
    if [ -n "$imp" ]; then
      if [ "${#imp}" -gt "$EG_FOLD_IMPACT_MAXB" ]; then
        imp="$(printf '%s' "$imp" | head -c "$EG_FOLD_IMPACT_MAXB" | sed '$d')"
      fi
      printf '\nRELATIONSHIPS FOR %s (callers, callees, type consumers, siblings; same index, no extra\nquery needed):\n%s\n' "$sym" "$imp"
    fi
  fi
}

"$EGQ" "$@" 2>&1 | { if [ "${1:-}" = "search" ]; then _fold; else cat; fi; } | sed \
  -e 's|^RELATED SITES (the same change usually also lands here):|RELATED SITES (graph-adjacent code; measured precision on this benchmark: 9% of these files are touched by a correct fix):|' \

exit "${PIPESTATUS[0]}"

**Two concrete findings, and one is a defect:**

```
payloads containing a CONTAINER MAP: 1 of 74 (1%)

GUESSING greps not already in the payload: 808
  a branch IS a real symbol in the repo index:  210 (26%)  <- a symbol list answers these
  a branch is a symbol in a GOLD file:           37 (5%)   <- a container map answers these
```

**The CONTAINER MAP appears in 1% of payloads.** The doctrine block I shipped in SHIP12 explicitly promises it — *"a CONTAINER MAP of that file (its extent and every member with line ranges, so you always know the exact range to read instead of guessing)"* — and it is essentially never emitted. So the doctrine advertised a feature the payload doesn't deliver, which is its own dead-flag-class defect and may be part of why SHIP12 went backwards: I told the agent to rely on something that wasn't there.

And the guessing greps are mostly **not** answerable by more payload: only 26% name a symbol that exists anywhere in the repo, and just 5% name one in a gold file. So **74% of guesses are for identifiers that don't exist** — the agent is probing a hypothesis and getting a negative answer. A container map can't pre-empt that; nothing can, except the agent seeing the real member list.

That gives an honest ceiling for this direction: 26% of 808 guesses ≈ 210 calls across 74 sessions ≈ **2.8 calls/session**, on top of the fold's ~6.6 in 39/88. Together roughly 9–12% — real, and still short of 15%.

So the two things worth doing next are clear, and one is free: fix the container-map emission so the doctrine stops promising vapour, and add a member-list block for the top hit's file (which is what would convert those 210 guesses).

I'll wait for DEF12's mechanism read before layering more, since its primary endpoint — calls-to-gold falling below the baseline's 3.62 — is the first honest test of whether making `search` terminal actually changes agent behaviour, and everything above is stacked on that assumption.

**`def-after-search` is 0.00 in the reference cell.** The pattern I built the fold to eliminate barely occurs. Going back to `tofix.py`, the sequence dump showed `eg:search -> eg:def -> eg:grep` at **2x out of 101 sessions** — I read a handful of rows in the tail of a distribution and treated them as the dominant shape. The actual dominant shape was `sh -> eg:search` at 20x, which is the agent orienting with a shell command *before* using the graph.

So I sized the fold from a different measurement (6.59 calls after a gold-naming payload, cause unattributed) and then justified it with a pattern occurring in ~5% of sessions. Those were two different things and I conflated them.

Also telling: `HOLD50/eg` makes **0.64 search calls per session** and the baseline makes 0. The graph is invoked less than once per session on average in the cell I've been treating as the reference — so "make search terminal" optimises a call that mostly doesn't happen.

Now the number is correct and cross-checked against `gq_calls.log` (2.71 transcript vs 3.30 log lines — the log counts wrapper retries). This is the decisive result:

```
graph calls / session        2.71
other calls displaced        2.65   (grep 1.24, Read 0.84, other sh 0.27, Edit 0.26, ...)
SUBSTITUTION RATIO           0.980  displaced per graph call
net call reduction          -0.06 / session   =  0.00%
RATIO NEEDED FOR 10%         3.281
```

The graph is a **1:1 substitute**. It swaps 2.65 calls for 2.71 calls, so it removes no work at all; the +2.49% comes entirely from the swapped calls being slightly cheaper. That single fact explains why eleven payload levers failed regardless of content.

Stacking every lever I have identified, at **perfect** effectiveness:

| lever | max msgs/session |
|---|---|
| already banked (+2.49%) | 2.03 |
| collapse graph call chains | 0.78 |
| grep source fold (G1) | 1.95 |
| fixable grep refinements (A+B+C) | 0.87 |
| **total** | **5.63 → 6.9%** |

At the 0.55 effectiveness every intervention actually achieves: **4.9%**. So 10% is not reachable from these pools even if all of them work perfectly.

The biggest untouched pool is `cat/sed` at 12.55/session, which the graph displaces **zero** of (eg 12.55 vs baseline 12.30). Displacing 6.18 of it needs each graph call to carry ~4.6 source windows ≈ 7 KB, which is 19 KB added to the prefix across 2.71 calls. On the two-axis model that costs +9.3% in re-read bytes against −8.6% in messages — **net worse**. That is the wall, and it is why the ratio is pinned near 1.0.

On the two easiest bins eg makes *more* calls than the baseline needed (22.0 vs 19.1, 42.2 vs 36.3): the agent runs its graph queries and then still does all the work the baseline did, because the baseline found the file in 19 calls without help. There was nothing to displace. On the hardest bin the same tool displaces 14.65 calls and wins 74% of pairs.

Three things that follow, which kill the fix attempts I have been making all session:

- **It is not a defect and not a class.** Graph usage is identical in winners and losers (2.68 vs 2.65, p=0.9128). Nothing in eg's behaviour distinguishes them, which is exactly why per-loser repair measured +0.04pt and why language, difficulty, and patch size all tested null.

- **Payload bytes cost about 4.5pt overall** (equal-weighted model −4.42% would become +0.07% if the payload were free), so bytes matter for the headline but not for the loss mechanism.

The one intervention this points at is arithmetically real: the graph's 2.65 calls are pure waste on the ~40% of instances that are easy, so calling it **once** instead of 2.65 times there would recover roughly 1.65 calls on a 19-call session. The blocker is that easiness is undetectable in advance, which I have measured directly: issue length correlates −0.038 with outcome and the same instance run twice correlates r=−0.022. The graph charges a fixed toll of about 2.65 calls and 5.5 KB per session. Its only benefit is displacing work the baseline would otherwise do. content.text:
Here is the full answer to both parts.

**What makes a task a winner or loser — and the brutal part: the task doesn't.**

```
                                  test-retest r    variance that is TASK
baseline calls (difficulty)          +0.276              46.1%
SAVINGS (win or lose)                +0.014               0%
```

Difficulty is about half a real property of the task. **Savings is not a property of the task at all** (r=+0.014 across 106 instances seen in two or more cells). The reason is arithmetic: savings is the *difference* between two runs, each carrying 54% run-level noise, so the difference is almost pure noise. The same instance wins in one cell and loses in the next.

Every pre-session signal I can extract is dead:

```
issue length     vs baseline calls r=-0.036   vs savings r=+0.025
issue lines                        r=-0.033             r=+0.012
has a stack trace                  r=+0.014             r=+0.048
file paths named in issue          r=-0.028             r=+0.032
code blocks in issue              r=+0.026             r=-0.076
repo identity                                  permutation p=0.1676  NO
```

The repo table looks convincing until you test it — jqlang +6.8% down to briannesbitt −25.1% is exactly the spread random grouping produces at n=15 to 27, p=0.17.

**Now your idea, priced properly.** "Graph only when needed" is a good instinct and it does help. I gave it a perfect oracle that knows the baseline's call count, which is information the tool can never have:

```
graph always                       +3.52%
gate: only if base > 29 calls      +4.45%   fires on 80% of tasks
gate: only if base > 43 calls      +6.62%   fires on 59%
gate: only if base > 53 calls      +7.70%   fires on 39%
gate: only if base > 69 calls      +8.30%   fires on 20%
gate on the realized outcome       +16.92%  (perfect hindsight, physically impossible)
```

So a **perfect difficulty oracle is worth +8.30%**, still under 10%, and the absolute ceiling of any gating scheme whatsoever — knowing the answer in advance — is +16.92%. Combined with the fact that no predictor exists above |r|=0.08, a real gate would capture a small fraction of that 8.30%.

There is one version of your idea that is implementable, because it needs no prediction at all — only patience. Instead of deciding at turn 0, don't offer the graph until the session has *already* run long, which is information available at runtime. That fires it on exactly the sessions where it wins and never pays the toll on the easy ones. Let me check whether the graph's displacement actually survives being deferred:

That closes it, and cleanly:

```
where the graph actually gets called
  median graph call is 5% into the session
  80.4% of calls land in the first quarter
  76.5% land in the first 10 tool calls
  median index of the FIRST graph call = 1   (the very first thing the agent does)

gate: suppress until call 10 -> keeps 23.5% of graph calls
gate: suppress until call 20 -> keeps 14.1%
gate: suppress until call 30 -> keeps  9.4%
```

The agent's first tool call *is* a graph call. So deferring the tool until a session proves itself hard throws away 90% of its usage, and the displacement goes with the toll. The runtime version of your idea does not survive contact with where the calls actually happen.

So, both parts answered:

**What makes a winner or loser:** not the task. Savings has a test-retest correlation of +0.014 — the same instance wins in one cell and loses in the next. What makes a winner is that the baseline *happened* to flail on that run, and 63% of the win/loss separation is baseline-side variance. Mechanically the graph charges a fixed 2.65 calls and its benefit is displacement, which runs from −0.09 per call on easy runs to +5.53 on hard ones.

**"Graph only when needed":** the right instinct, and the highest-value direction anyone has measured here. A perfect difficulty oracle is worth +8.30%, and perfect hindsight is worth +16.92% — compare that with 6.9% from every payload lever stacked. The problem is purely that the signal does not exist at decision time: my pre-session features all came in under |r|=0.08, repo identity tests p=0.17, and a runtime gate arrives too late to matter.

One honest qualification, because it is the only door I found that is not closed: **46.1% of difficulty variance is genuinely task-level.** That is an upper bound on what any difficulty predictor could reach, and my hand-built features (issue length, stack traces, paths named, code blocks, repo) captured essentially none of it. A learned predictor over the issue text plus repo structure is not ruled out by anything I measured — it is just unbuilt. That would be a real project, not a config change, and its ceiling is 8.30%, not 15%.

Recorded in memory and in the notepad handoff.

The summary of where this leaves us:

**Losers are easy tasks, not broken tasks.** The graph opens the session with a query (median first graph call is tool call #1), pays 2.65 calls, and on the 40% of instances where the baseline finds the file in under 43 calls there is simply nothing for it to displace. Same tool, same behaviour, no bug: usage in losers is statistically identical to winners at p=0.9128.

**Your gating instinct is the best direction found in this campaign**, and I can now put a price on it: +8.30% with a perfect difficulty oracle, +16.92% with impossible hindsight, against 6.9% for every payload lever stacked together. It fails not on value but on information — savings has zero task-level signal (r=+0.014), every pre-session feature lands under |r|=0.08, and a runtime gate arrives after 90% of the graph calls have already happened.

The one thing I did not close, and I want to be precise rather than encouraging: 46.1% of *difficulty* variance is genuinely task-level, so a learned predictor over issue text and repo structure is not ruled out by any measurement I made. My hand-built features captured essentially none of it. That is a real modelling project with a hard ceiling of +8.30%, so it reaches your earlier 10% target only if paired with something else, and it does not reach 15% at all.

Two accounting notes so nothing here gets misquoted later: the +8.30% and +16.92% figures are conditioned on one arm's outcome, so they are upper bounds and not reportable results. And the honest unconditioned number at n=489 is pooled +3.52%, equal-weighted −6.64%, median −0.08%, win rate 49.9% — with correctness still ungraded per your rule.
make a plan to hit 10%

Let me ground this plan in numbers rather than intentions, since unquantified stages are exactly what has failed all session. Two computations decide whether a 10% plan can even be written. First: how accurate would a difficulty predictor have to be, given a perfect one is only worth 8.30%?

# Plan: hit 10% graph token savings via a zero-toll difficulty gate

Written 2026-08-11. Replaces the 20% resolution-gateway plan, which its own S0 offline gate closed
(21-26% displacement measured against the 30% it required). Target metric is **pooled total tokens**
(user decision). Gate-as-product accepted (user decision).

## Context

The goal is 10% graph savings, fairly. Today, on 556 paired gated instances pooled across every cell
on disk: **tokens +6.22%, cost +4.61%** (median +2.35% / +2.78%, equal-weighted negative).

Why every previous plan failed, now measured rather than guessed:

```
graph calls/session          2.71        (transcript, cross-checked vs gq_calls.log 3.30)
other calls displaced        2.65
SUBSTITUTION RATIO           0.980       <- a 1:1 substitute removes no work by construction
net call reduction          -0.06/session
```

entire-graph swaps 2.65 shell calls for 2.71 graph calls. The +6.22% comes from the swapped calls
being cheaper, not from a shorter session. That single fact explains why eleven payload levers all
failed independent of their content, and why every lever stacked at *perfect* effectiveness tops out
at 6.9% cost.

The loss mechanism is not a defect. Split by how much the no-tool baseline flails:

```
baseline calls  eg calls  base calls  displacement  ratio/call  win rate   cost delta
    2-29          22.0       19.1        -0.25       -0.09       37.1%     -21.71%
   30-43          42.2       36.3        -3.25       -1.23       42.3%     -18.32%
   43-53          50.9       48.5        +0.25       +0.09       41.2%      -8.78%
   53-69          61.7       60.1        +1.05       +0.40       53.6%      -3.31%
  69-136          73.0       85.0       +14.65       +5.53       74.3%     +17.91%
```

Losers are **easy tasks**. The graph pays its 2.65-call toll and displaces nothing, because the
baseline found the file in 19 calls unaided. Graph usage in losers is statistically identical to
winners (2.68 vs 2.65, permutation **p=0.9128**) — there is no behaviour to repair, which is why
per-loser fixes measured +0.04pt. The two-axis model
(`1.31*ln(calls) + 0.49*ln(bytes)`) reproduces the **sign in all five bins**.

So the only lever with real headroom is **not paying the toll on easy tasks**.

## The arithmetic, and why this plan stops where it does

Noisy-oracle simulation (40 seeds per cell, gate fires on the top fraction by predicted difficulty),
where `rho` is the predictor's correlation with true baseline effort:

```
rho    fire20%   fire40%   fire60%   fire80%  fire100%
0.0     +0.92     +1.41     +2.07     +2.80     +3.53     (cost %)
0.5     +4.08     +5.14     +5.12     +4.58     +3.53
0.68    ~+5.2     +6.40     +5.7      +4.8      +3.53
1.0     +8.29     +7.51     +6.68     +4.45     +3.53
```

**Gating alone cannot reach 10% at any rho** (max +8.29% cost even with a perfect oracle). And rho is
itself capped: only **46.1%** of baseline-effort variance is task-level (test-retest r=+0.276 across
106 instances seen in 2+ cells), so a perfect task-level predictor is bounded at
rho = sqrt(0.461) = **0.68**.

Second, independent lever. The payload is 76.1% source body, and that body is sometimes paid twice:

```
files shown with a body in a payload   4.17/session
of those, agent LATER read the file    35.0%
lines shown that were re-read anyway   58.0%   -> 2,466 B/session of pure waste
```

Combining the two (independent mechanisms, tokens = 1.35x cost leverage measured on the same pairs):

| build | cost | tokens |
|---|---|---|
| today | +4.61% | +6.22% |
| gate rho=0.50 + body cap | +6.80% | +9.18% |
| **gate rho=0.60 + body cap** | **+7.50%** | **+10.13%** |
| gate rho=0.68 (max buildable) + body cap | +8.06% | +10.88% |
| perfect oracle + full body trim | +11.19% | +15.10% |

**The plan needs rho >= 0.60**, i.e. the predictor must capture (0.60/0.68)^2 = **78% of all
available task-level signal**. That is the whole bet and S0 tests it for $0.

## Design

**1. Zero-toll difficulty gate.** The gate must not cost an agent turn, or it eats its own margin
(one graph call on 60% of non-fired tasks is a 0.74pt drag). So it runs in the harness **before
turn 1**, consulting the graph index directly — never as a tool call.

Features, all computable pre-session from `problem.txt` plus one direct index query (no agent
message): the retrieval score distribution of the issue-derived query (top-1 score, top1-top5 gap,
score entropy over top-10, number of distinct files in the top-10, whether any symbol named in the
issue resolves in the index), plus repo scale (indexed symbol count, file count). The score
distribution is the load-bearing feature and it is the graph's own machinery: a sharply-peaked
ranking means the task is localizable, hence easy, hence the graph will not pay off.

Hand-built *text* features are already known dead and are not in this list: issue length r=-0.036,
lines -0.033, stack trace +0.014, paths named -0.028, code blocks +0.026, repo identity p=0.1676.

**2. Body cap, no prediction required.** Re-read files have disproportionately large spans (35% of
files but 58% of lines), so capping each shown body at N lines cuts preferentially from the wasted
ones. N is chosen in S0 by simulation, not guessed.

Files to modify:
- `tools/_eggate.py` (new) — feature extraction + fitted gate, mirroring the structure of the
  existing `tools/_eglit.py` / `tools/_egsiblings.py` helpers
- `tools/eg-q` — read `EG_GATE` / `EG_BODY_CAP`; the wrapper already has the `_grep_ctx` / `_fold_impact`
  fold points to hook into
- `tools/run_3arm.sh` — invoke the gate before the eg arm's first turn and, when it says "skip",
  emit the eg arm with an empty `tool_block.txt` (identical config to baseline)
- `logs/gatefit.py`, `logs/score_g10.py` (new scorers), reusing `logs/cost.py`, `logs/prices.py`,
  `logs/loserwhy.py`'s gate+pair loader, `logs/contam.sh` for patch hygiene

## Fairness

The gate reads only the issue text and the graph's own index, ships **no instructions**, and the
baseline arm is untouched. On non-fired tasks the eg arm runs with an empty tool block, i.e. the
identical configuration to baseline. Passes the project rule ("would this sentence help an arm with
no tool?" — there is no sentence). No `PROMPT_CLAMP_DECLARED` needed.

Pre-scoring gate, every cell: `prompt_invariant` matches across arms except the eg tool block;
baseline `tool_block.txt` is 0 B; `grep -c VERIFY tools/eg-q` = 0; `logs/contam.sh` reports 0
contaminated patches; reject any `CORRUPT_CC_OUT` record (a `GUIDE30B/baseline/gson-2479`-class
record passed both gates before).

**Mandatory disclosure in any writeup:** part of this gain is *avoided losses*, not added value, and
the tool declines to engage on ~60% of tasks. The headline must read "entire-graph with automatic
gating: tokens +X%, engaging on Y% of tasks".

## Stages

**S0. Offline feasibility, $0.** Fit the gate on the 556 existing pairs using only pre-session
features; report **cross-validated** rho against baseline effort (grouped CV by instance, so the
same instance never spans train and test). Simulate the body cap over stored payloads to pick N and
measure recovered bytes. Combine both through the two-axis model.
**Exit bar: projected tokens >= 10.0% at the cross-validated rho.** If rho < 0.60, stop and report
the shortfall with the number — do not spend.

**S1. Build**, both behind flags defaulting OFF. Verify by rendering an actual payload and an actual
prompt, never by reading source: `EG_LITERALS` and `EG_SIBLINGS` were silent no-ops in every cell
ever run because their helper files did not exist, and I shipped a cosmetic `ARTIFACT_EXCLUDES` array
that was never wired in.

**S2. Delivery smoke, n=4, ~$25.** Gate fires on 4/4 predicted-hard and 0/4 predicted-easy; the
skipped arm's `tool_block.txt` is 0 B; body cap present in rendered payloads; bytes <= budget.

**S3. Mechanism cell, n=30, ~$180.** PRIMARY endpoints, pre-registered, both arm-internal:
gate precision/recall against realized baseline effort, and eg payload bytes/session falling from
5,590 B. **Tokens are secondary and not claim-bearing at this stage** — this is the discipline that
caught CS50's false +12.84% (it scored positive while `locate_symbol` rose).

**S4. rep50 confirmation, n=50, ~$300**, only if S3's primary clears. Sealed prereg with the band
above written first. Report pooled **and** median **and** equal-weighted **and** cluster-bootstrap
CI, with the mechanism beside them, in both tokens and cost.

**S5. Grade both arms** (`FAIL_TO_PASS`), only after the 10% token bar is met, per the standing rule.
Withholding the tool on 60% of tasks could cost resolution; noninferiority within 3pt or the token
win does not count.

## Verification

Per stage: S0 grouped cross-validated rho printed with n and a permutation p-value; S2 assertions on
emitted `prompt.txt` and `tool_block.txt`; S3/S4 the fairness gate above runs **before** any number
is read, then `logs/score_g10.py` for mechanism and `logs/cost.py` for tokens and cost; S5 resolved
rate on identical instances both arms.

## Honest assessment

**Floor +9.18% tokens (rho=0.50), target +10.13% (rho=0.60), ceiling +10.88% (rho=0.68).** The 10%
bar sits *inside* this band but not at its floor, so this plan can fail honestly and I have written
the failure number down in advance.

Two named risks. First, rho: the predictor must capture 78% of available task-level signal, and
every hand-built feature I have tried captured essentially none — the entire bet rests on the
retrieval-score distribution carrying signal that text features do not. S0 settles it for $0.
Second, the ER12 precedent: payload widening projected 2.11 displaced reads and delivered 0.42, so
the body cap's simulated value should be treated as an upper bound.

What would make me stop and report instead of spending: S0's cross-validated rho below 0.60, or S3's
gate precision no better than chance. I am not promising 10%; I am committing to a pre-registered
shot at it with a $0 gate in front of the money, and to reporting the shortfall in the same terms if
it misses.

ranking means the task is localizable, hence easy, hence the graph will not pay off.

Hand-built *text* features are already known dead and are not in this list: issue length r=-0.036,
lines -0.033, stack trace +0.014, paths named -0.028, code blocks +0.026, repo identity p=0.1676.

**2. Body cap, no prediction required.** Re-read files have disproportionately large spans (35% of
files but 58% of lines), so capping each shown body at N lines cuts preferentially from the wasted
ones. N is chosen in S0 by simulation, not guessed.

Files to modify:
- `tools/_eggate.py` (new) — feature extraction + fitted gate, mirroring the structure of the
  existing `tools/_eglit.py` / `tools/_egsiblings.py` helpers
- `tools/eg-q` — read `EG_GATE` / `EG_BODY_CAP`; the wrapper already has the `_grep_ctx` / `_fold_impact`
  fold points to hook into
- `tools/run_3arm.sh` — invoke the gate before the eg arm's first turn and, when it says "skip",
  emit the eg arm with an empty `tool_block.txt` (identical config to baseline)
- `logs/gatefit.py`, `logs/score_g10.py` (new scorers), reusing `logs/cost.py`, `logs/prices.py`,
  `logs/loserwhy.py`'s gate+pair loader, `logs/contam.sh` for patch hygiene

## Fairness

The gate reads only the issue text and the graph's own index, ships **no instructions**, and the
baseline arm is untouched. On non-fired tasks the eg arm runs with an empty tool block, i.e. the
identical configuration to baseline. Passes the project rule ("would this sentence help an arm with
no tool?" — there is no sentence). No `PROMPT_CLAMP_DECLARED` needed.

Pre-scoring gate, every cell: `prompt_invariant` matches across arms except the eg tool block;
baseline `tool_block.txt` is 0 B; `grep -c VERIFY tools/eg-q` = 0; `logs/contam.sh` reports 0
contaminated patches; reject any `CORRUPT_CC_OUT` record (a `GUIDE30B/baseline/gson-2479`-class
record passed both gates before).

**Mandatory disclosure in any writeup:** part of this gain is *avoided losses*, not added value, and
the tool declines to engage on ~60% of tasks. The headline must read "entire-graph with automatic
gating: tokens +X%, engaging on Y% of tasks".

## Stages

**S0. Offline feasibility, $0.** Fit the gate on the 556 existing pairs using only pre-session
features; report **cross-validated** rho against baseline effort (grouped CV by instance, so the
same instance never spans train and test). Simulate the body cap over stored payloads to pick N and
measure recovered bytes. Combine both through the two-axis model.
**Exit bar: projected tokens >= 10.0% at the cross-validated rho.** If rho < 0.60, stop and report
the shortfall with the number — do not spend.

**S1. Build**, both behind flags defaulting OFF. Verify by rendering an actual payload and an actual
prompt, never by reading source: `EG_LITERALS` and `EG_SIBLINGS` were silent no-ops in every cell
ever run because their helper files did not exist, and I shipped a cosmetic `ARTIFACT_EXCLUDES` array
that was never wired in.

**S2. Delivery smoke, n=4, ~$25.** Gate fires on 4/4 predicted-hard and 0/4 predicted-easy; the
skipped arm's `tool_block.txt` is 0 B; body cap present in rendered payloads; bytes <= budget.

**S3. Mechanism cell, n=30, ~$180.** PRIMARY endpoints, pre-registered, both arm-internal:
gate precision/recall against realized baseline effort, and eg payload bytes/session falling from
5,590 B. **Tokens are secondary and not claim-bearing at this stage** — this is the discipline that
caught CS50's false +12.84% (it scored positive while `locate_symbol` rose).

**S4. rep50 confirmation, n=50, ~$300**, only if S3's primary clears. Sealed prereg with the band
above written first. Report pooled **and** median **and** equal-weighted **and** cluster-bootstrap
CI, with the mechanism beside them, in both tokens and cost.

**S5. Grade both arms** (`FAIL_TO_PASS`), only after the 10% token bar is met, per the standing rule.
Withholding the tool on 60% of tasks could cost resolution; noninferiority within 3pt or the token
win does not count.

## Verification

Per stage: S0 grouped cross-validated rho printed with n and a permutation p-value; S2 assertions on
emitted `prompt.txt` and `tool_block.txt`; S3/S4 the fairness gate above runs **before** any number
is read, then `logs/score_g10.py` for mechanism and `logs/cost.py` for tokens and cost; S5 resolved
rate on identical instances both arms.

## Honest assessment

**Floor +9.18% tokens (rho=0.50), target +10.13% (rho=0.60), ceiling +10.88% (rho=0.68).** The 10%
bar sits *inside* this band but not at its floor, so this plan can fail honestly and I have written
the failure number down in advance.

Two named risks. First, rho: the predictor must capture 78% of available task-level signal, and
every hand-built feature I have tried captured essentially none — the entire bet rests on the
retrieval-score distribution carrying signal that text features do not. S0 settles it for $0.
Second, the ER12 precedent: payload widening projected 2.11 displaced reads and delivered 0.42, so
the body cap's simulated value should be treated as an upper bound.

What would make me stop and report instead of spending: S0's cross-validated rho below 0.60, or S3's
gate precision no better than chance. I am not promising 10%; I am committing to a pre-registered
shot at it with a $0 gate in front of the money, and to reporting the shortfall in the same terms if
it misses.

Here is the plain answer to both questions.

## What makes a task a winner or a loser

Every task is a race between two runs of the same agent. One run has the graph, one does not. The graph costs about 2.65 extra tool calls per session, and it earns that back only by saving the other run's wasted searching. So the whole outcome comes down to one thing: **did the run without the graph waste any time?**

I sorted all 489 tasks by how much work the no-graph run needed:

| work the no-graph run needed | graph run | no-graph run | who wins | result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 to 29 calls | 22.0 | 19.1 | graph loses | −21.7% |
| 30 to 43 | 42.2 | 36.3 | graph loses | −18.3% |
| 43 to 53 | 50.9 | 48.5 | roughly even | −8.8% |
| 53 to 69 | 61.7 | 60.1 | roughly even | −3.3% |
| 69 to 136 | 73.0 | 85.0 | graph wins | +17.9% |

Read the first row carefully, because it is the whole story. On easy tasks the no-graph run found the file in 19 calls. The graph run used 22. It ran its graph searches **and then still did all the same work anyway**, because there was nothing to skip. The graph got charged and delivered nothing, so it lost 21.7%.

Now the last row. Here the no-graph run flailed for 85 calls. The graph run finished in 73. Same tool, same behaviour, but this time there was 12 calls of wasted searching to prevent, so it won 17.9%.

**Losers are easy tasks. Winners are hard tasks.** Nothing is broken in the losers. I checked whether the graph behaves differently when it loses, and it does not: it makes 2.68 calls in winners and 2.65 in losers, which is a statistical dead heat. There is no bug in those sessions to fix. That is why all my attempts to repair the losers produced almost exactly zero.

The uncomfortable part: **whether a task is easy is mostly luck, not a property of the task.** I found 106 tasks that were run in more than one experiment. How hard a task turned out to be repeated only weakly between runs, and whether the graph won or lost did not repeat at all. Run the same task twice and it wins once, loses once. Slightly less than half of the "difficulty" is a real property of the task; the rest is the agent having a good or bad day.

## Your idea: only use the graph when needed

This is the right instinct, and it is the best idea anyone has had on this problem. I measured what it is worth by giving it a **perfect** crystal ball that already knows how hard each task will be:

| rule | savings | how often the graph fires |
|---|---|---|
| always use the graph | +3.5% | 100% |
| only if the task needs 29+ calls | +4.5% | 80% |
| only if 43+ | +6.6% | 59% |
| only if 53+ | +7.7% | 39% |
| only if 69+ | +8.3% | 20% |
| perfect hindsight, impossible | +16.9% | — |

So even with a perfect crystal ball the idea gives **8.3%**. That is a lot better than anything else I have tried, and it still does not reach 10% on its own.

Then there is the harder problem: building the crystal ball. Everything obvious fails. Issue length, whether the issue has an error trace, how many file names the issue mentions, how much code is in the issue, which repository it is: all of them are essentially uncorrelated with difficulty. The repository looked promising at first, with one repo at +6.8% and another at −25.1%, until I tested it and found that spread is exactly what you get from shuffling tasks into random groups.

I also tried the version that needs no crystal ball at all: just wait, and only turn the graph on once a session has clearly gone long. That fails for a simple reason. **The agent's very first tool call is usually a graph call**, and three quarters of all graph calls happen in the first ten calls. If you make the graph wait until call 30, you throw away 90% of its use, and the benefit leaves along with the cost.

## So how the plan reaches 10%

Gating alone tops out at 8.3%, so the plan pairs it with a second, unrelated saving. The graph's answer includes chunks of source code, and I measured that in 35% of cases the agent goes and reads that same file anyway. Those bytes get paid for twice. Trimming that waste is worth another 1.7%.

Gate plus trim comes to about 8.1% in dollars and **10.9% in tokens**, which is why you chose tokens as the measure. The gap between the two is real and I will keep stating both: the graph's savings sit mostly in cheap cached text, so it saves more raw tokens than dollars.

The one thing that has to be true, and which I am testing right now for zero dollars before spending anything: the crystal ball has to work. Not perfectly, but it has to reach about 60% of perfect. My plan is to build it from the graph's own search scores rather than from the issue text, on the theory that when the graph's top result stands out sharply from the rest, the task is easy to locate and the graph will not pay off. That test is running now. If it comes back too weak, I will tell you the number and stop rather than spend $500 on a run I already know will miss.

S0 fails its exit bar, and the reason matters. Out-of-fold rho = **+0.193** against the 0.60 required, and the fitted gate is worth *less than no gate at all* (firing on 60% gives +4.18% tokens versus +4.49% for always firing).

Those are not task properties — they describe **which verb the agent chose first**, which is leakage from agent behaviour and is not available before turn 1 anyway. The score features the plan was betting on came in at top1 +0.099 and gap +0.012.

S0 did its job: it cost nothing and stopped a $505 spend. The result, plainly:

**The gate fails.** Cross-validated rho is **+0.193** against the 0.60 the plan required, folds split by instance. The fitted gate is worth **+0.10 percentage points** over just always using the graph. The features that carried signal turned out to be leakage — `is_search` (+0.302) describes which verb the agent picked first, which is not knowable before turn 1. The retrieval-score features had exactly the sign my design predicted (`top1` −0.164: a sharply-peaked ranking does mean an easy task) but at a quarter of the needed strength.

**And S0 caught an error in my own plan.** I credited the body trim at +1.66% cost / +2.24% tokens. That figure came from the 2,466 B/session of source bodies the agent re-read anyway — but knowing *which* bodies those are in advance is another prediction problem, so I had counted a prediction-dependent quantity as free. The genuinely free subset is bodies shown twice for the same file: 420 B/session, worth **+0.38% tokens**. Capping bodies harder does cut more (+1.13% at 10 lines) but removes 22.8% of the payload and would force the reads it was meant to prevent.

```
honest total for the approved plan
  today (n=556)     tokens +6.22%    cost +4.61%
  + best gate               +0.10pt
  + safe dedupe             +0.38pt
  TOTAL                    ~+6.7% tokens      <- against a 10% target
```

**G1 also finished** — 24/24, 10 gated pairs: cost **−9.50%**, tokens **−8.59%**. The isolated grep-source-fold lever lost. At n=10 that sits inside my measured noise floor of ~8.6% between identical cells, so it is not conclusive, but nothing about it supports the lever.

So the approved route does not reach 10%, and I am reporting that rather than running S1 through S4 into a wall I can already see.

That leaves exactly one option with enough headroom, and now that tokens is the agreed metric the arithmetic changed in its favour: **routing shell `grep` through the graph**. Intercepted commands pay no message toll, which lifts graph-touched calls from 2.71 to about 14.6 per session — the only denominator large enough to matter. It computes to roughly +9.6% cost, which at the measured 1.35x token leverage is about **+13% tokens**. That clears 10%.

The single blocker has never been fairness — the shim ships no instructions and the baseline keeps real grep, so it passes the project rule. It is that the saving would belong to "Entire-backed grep" rather than "the code graph," and the other agent's plan lists the shim under do-not-ship for that reason. You accepted gate-as-product on the same kind of reasoning, so I think you may well accept this one, but it changes what the headline claims and I will not relabel the product on my own.

Say the word and I will write the prereg for it with the honest label and run it. Everything else I have measured is closed.

I derived it from the message axis alone, assuming each intercepted grep displaces about one call. My own measurements say the displaceable pool is much smaller than that, and graph output may be **fatter** than raw grep output, which would cost bytes. Auditing both sides first:

The shim audit changes the picture in an important way, and it is better than I said. Note that the byte cost is small (graph-grep is 1,286 B/call vs shell grep's 1,146 B, so only −1.33%), but the displaceable pool I used as the bound excludes the biggest piece:

```
shim intercepts        14.56 shell greps/session at 1,146 B
replaced with          graph-grep at 1,286 B  ->  byte axis only -1.33% cost
displaceable pool I bounded it with:
  fixable refinements   0.87
  grep -> follow-up read 1.95
  TOTAL                 2.82   -> even at PERFECT effectiveness only +6.16% cost
```

That 2.82 bound **deliberately excludes the 3.43 wrong-guess greps per session** — the 62% of refinements where the agent tried a completely different string. I excluded them because better output for a *wrong pattern* cannot help. But a graph-backed grep is exactly the thing that can answer a wrong pattern, by falling back to semantically related symbols when the literal match misses. Include that pool and the projection clears 10% tokens even at 20% realisation.

So the whole decision rests on one untested assumption. Testing it for $0 — when the agent's literal guess missed, did the graph already know the file the agent eventually needed?

content.text:
S0g kills the shim, and it does so by exposing the flaw in my own projection. The number that matters:

```
shell/Grep calls                       14.81/session
  returned effectively NOTHING          1.34/session  (9.1%)
  machine-parsing mode (-q/-c/-l/-o)    2.26/session  (shim must stay silent)
  SHIM WOULD SAFELY FIRE                1.07/session  (7.2%)

wrong-guess transitions                 6,043
  where the PRIOR grep was EMPTY        520  (8.6%)
```

**Only 8.6% of wrong guesses follow a grep that returned nothing.** The other 91.4% follow a grep that *did* return hits — the agent got results, they were not useful, so it tried a different string. So a safe miss-only trigger reaches **0.18 calls/session** of the 2.09 addressable pool, worth +0.19 to +0.33 points. Against the 643 B/session of hint text, that nets to roughly zero or slightly negative.

And the `literal only` rows in that table are not reachable by this design either. That pool (0.87 fixable refinements plus 1.95 grep-then-read) consists entirely of greps that **succeeded** — you read the file your grep just found. A miss-only shim never fires on them. To capture them the shim would have to rewrite the output of *successful* greps, which is both the build-breaking design and the one thing already measured: G1's source fold did exactly that and came back **−9.50%**.

So the shim fails S0 too. My +9.6% estimate assumed every intercepted grep displaces work; the audit shows the displaceable events almost never coincide with a condition it is safe to trigger on.

I ran the plan. Every stage gate held, and all of them failed, for a total spend of **$0**.

**S0, the difficulty gate.** Cross-validated rho **+0.193** against the 0.60 required. The fitted gate is worth **+0.10 points** over just always using the graph. The features that carried signal were leakage — `is_search` (+0.302) describes which verb the agent picked first, not a property of the task.

**S0d, the payload trim.** This caught an error in my own approved plan. I had credited it at +2.24% tokens using the 2,466 B/session of bodies the agent re-read anyway, but identifying those in advance is another prediction problem, so I had counted a prediction-dependent quantity as free. The genuinely free part is **+0.38%**.

**S0e through S0g, the grep shim.** This one looked like it worked twice before failing. 30.8% of wrong-guess greps target a file the graph had already named; the causal version held at 28.9%. Then the trigger audit: **91.4% of wrong guesses follow a grep that returned hits**, not one that missed. A shim can only be made safe by firing on a miss, so it reaches 0.18 of the 2.09 addressable calls per session, which nets to zero or slightly negative after its own 643 B of hint text. The remaining pool consists entirely of *successful* greps, and rewriting those is what G1 did — **−9.50% cost, −8.59% tokens**.

```
honest position, n=556 paired gated
  today                    tokens +6.22%    cost +4.61%    wall-clock -7.9%
  + best gate                     +0.10pt
  + safe dedupe                   +0.38pt
  + safe grep shim                ~0.00pt (possibly negative)
  TOTAL                    tokens ~+6.7%    against a 10% target
```

**I cannot get to 10% and I no longer have a candidate that isn't already measured as failing.** The reason is the same one throughout: entire-graph is a 1:1 substitute, displacing 0.980 calls per call it makes, so it makes sessions slightly cheaper rather than shorter. Gating is the highest-value idea available and its perfect-oracle ceiling is 8.3%, which no buildable predictor comes near.

Two things I want to state plainly rather than leave buried, because they change what the honest headline is:

**The graph is 7.9% slower in wall-clock** — 127.0 hours versus 117.7 across 1,175 sessions. A user feels that; they do not feel the tokens. The correct pair to quote is tokens +6.22% *and* wall-clock −7.9%, and I had been giving you only the first half.

**Correctness is still ungraded**, per your rule, so none of these numbers are known to preserve resolution rate.

What I have not done is spend your money on a cell whose result I could already compute. If you want a number on the board instead, the one route I have not tested is enriching *every* grep rather than only misses — but G1 is the closest measurement of that and it lost 9.50%, so I would be running it expecting to lose, and I would rather you decide that knowingly than have me quietly do it.

Confirmed the bug precisely: `WorktreeMatchesHEAD` runs `git status --porcelain --untracked-files=all` and requires **completely empty output**, so a single untracked `.DS_Store` or compiled binary disables the search cache for the entire repo. That is why my checkout pays 9 seconds per search.

8	// WorktreeMatchesHEAD reports whether the working tree's indexable content is
9	// byte-identical to the committed HEAD tree.
10	//
11	// It is the precondition that lets a caller reuse a tree-keyed index cache for
12	// a working-tree query: when nothing is modified, staged, deleted or untracked,
13	// every file a working-tree walk can see is exactly the file HEAD records, so a
14	// snapshot built from one is a snapshot of the other.
15	//
16	// The check is one `git status --porcelain --untracked-files=all` and is
17	// deliberately conservative:
18	//
19	//   - it reports FALSE on any output at all — modified, staged, deleted,
20	//     renamed, unmerged, untracked, or a dirty submodule;
21	//   - `--untracked-files=all` is required, not optional: a working-tree walk
22	//     indexes untracked-but-not-ignored files, so "no tracked modifications"
23	//     alone would not make the two views equal;
24	//   - files git ignores are excluded from BOTH sides (the provider's
25	//     working-tree walk honours .gitignore), so an ignored build artifact
26	//     changing cannot invalidate the equality. If the ignore rules themselves
27	//     change so that a file stops being ignored, that file becomes untracked
28	//     and this check turns false, which is the safe direction;
29	//   - any error (not a git repository, git missing) reports FALSE with the
30	//     error, never a hopeful TRUE.
31	//
32	// `--no-optional-locks` keeps this read-only probe from refreshing the index
33	// and so from contending with a concurrent git command in the same repo.
34	func WorktreeMatchesHEAD(ctx context.Context, repo string) (bool, error) {
35		// A repository with no commits has no HEAD tree to be equal to.

37			return false, err
38		}

40			"--no-optional-locks", "status", "--porcelain", "--untracked-files=all", "-z")
41		if err != nil {
42			return false, err
43		}
44		return strings.Trim(out, "\x00\n\r \t") == "", nil

## What

`worktreeSnapshotCacheable` required a **wholly pristine** working tree before it would reuse a tree-keyed index. It asked `WorktreeMatchesHEAD`, which is a plain `git status --porcelain --untracked-files=all` compared against empty output. So a single file no parser ever opens — a `.DS_Store`, a compiled binary, a log, an editor swap file — disabled the search cache for the **entire repository**, and every query re-indexed from scratch.

A path that cannot contribute a symbol or a relation cannot make a snapshot stale, so it is not a reason to throw one away.

## Measured, on this repo

```
with a .DS_Store present
  run 1: cache_hit=False  index_ms=3704   total_ms=4480
  run 2: cache_hit=True   index_ms=131    total_ms=908
  run 3: cache_hit=True   index_ms=126    total_ms=887

control, untracked .go present (must NOT cache)
  run 1: cache_hit=False  index_ms=3598
  run 2: cache_hit=False  index_ms=3675
```

28x on index latency, 5x on total, and the control still bypasses correctly. Before the change the first case behaved like the control: never cached. On the working checkout this was `index_cache_hit=false` with `index_latency_ms=9062` on a back-to-back repeat of the same query.

## How

- `gitutil` gains **`WorktreeDirtyPaths`**, the factual list of paths that diverge from HEAD. `WorktreeMatchesHEAD` becomes `len(paths)==0` and keeps its exact contract, so its existing callers and tests are unaffected. Both sides of a rename are reported, since porcelain `-z` spends a second record on the source path and that record has no status prefix of its own.
- `worktreeSnapshotCacheable` forgives a dirty path only when **`extensionUnsupported`** says so — the same predicate the indexer uses to skip a file, so the two cannot disagree about what is read.

## Why this is safe

- **Conservative on extensionless paths.** `extensionUnsupported` treats them as supported, because a shebang can make one a script. A stray binary named `entire-graph` (no extension) therefore still bypasses the cache. That is deliberate, and asserted in a test.
- **Per-path, not a blanket "ignore untracked".** One indexable untracked file still bypasses, even alongside four unindexable ones.
- **`.gitignore` edits are forgiven, and that is sound.** Ignore rules can only change whether *untracked* files are walked, and an untracked file that is indexable already fails the gate on its own. So no combination of ignore-rule change plus untracked file can serve a stale snapshot.
- **Ignored files were already out of scope** — git omits them without `--ignored`, matching the provider's working-tree walk.

## Tests

- `TestWorktreeDirtyPaths` — clean / untracked / modified / **renamed (both paths)** / ignored, and asserts `WorktreeMatchesHEAD == (len(paths)==0)` in every case.
- `TestWorktreeSnapshotStillCachesWithUnindexableUntrackedFiles` — four unindexable untracked files keep the cache warm with an **identical symbol set**; an extensionless file still bypasses; an untracked `.go` still bypasses and is still indexed.
- The pre-existing `TestWorktreeSnapshotBypassesCacheForUntrackedFiles` (untracked `.go`) is unchanged and still passes.

`gofmt` clean, `go vet` clean, `go build ./...` clean, full `./internal/gitutil` and `./internal/sem` suites pass.

## Context

Found while measuring entire-graph's wall-clock cost on a benchmark: across 1,175 paired agent sessions the graph arm ran **7.9% slower** than the no-tool arm (127.0 h vs 117.7 h) while saving tokens. A never-hitting index cache is one contributor — an agent's checkout almost always has some untracked scratch file in it, so in practice the cache was off far more often than intended.

Done. Both PRs are open, the harness is back to its clean state, and the other agent is notified.

**entire-graph — https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph/pull/92**

A real performance bug, found while measuring why the graph is slower in wall-clock. `worktreeSnapshotCacheable` demanded a wholly pristine working tree before reusing an index, so a single `.DS_Store` or compiled binary disabled the search cache for the whole repository and every query re-indexed.

```
with a .DS_Store present
  run 1: cache_hit=False  index_ms=3704  total_ms=4480
  run 2: cache_hit=True   index_ms=131   total_ms=908     28x index, 5x total
control, untracked .go (must NOT cache)
  run 1/2: cache_hit=False  index_ms=3598 / 3675
```

It forgives only paths `extensionUnsupported` rejects — the indexer's own predicate, so the two cannot disagree about what gets read. Extensionless paths stay conservative because a shebang can make one a script. `gofmt`, `go vet`, `go build ./...` clean; full `gitutil` and `sem` suites pass.

**graphmark — https://github.com/entirehq/graphmark/pull/70**

`collect_patch.sh` had lowercase-only repro filters and no `out/` exclusion, so `Repro.java` and compiled `.class` files graded as the model's answer. Verified on a synthetic tree: a one-line Java fix beside `Repro.java`, `out/classes/*.class` and `explore_thing.py` now yields a 245-byte patch containing only the fix, all four assertions passing. Plus `analysis/savings/` with the 13 scorers, so the decomposition is reproducible instead of re-derived.

**Harness reverted.** `tools/eg-q` is back to the fold-free 1,268-byte wrapper, with zero sessions live and an atomic move, backup kept. Both folds I had added measured negative in isolation — grep-source-fold −9.50%, impact-fold −0.6% — so removing them *is* the best honest state. `grep -c VERIFY tools/eg-q` is 0.

Three things worth flagging about how I scoped this:

**I did not ship what I could not stand behind.** The local graphmark checkout had modifications to `run_3arm.sh` that are someone else's experimental tool-block work; sweeping those into my PR would have attributed them to me and shipped untested changes to a shared file. Same for `_eglit.py` and `_egsiblings.py` — they fix genuinely dead flags, but neither was ever measured to help, so they stay out.

**Two real defects are named in the PR rather than fixed.** The gate accepts `CORRUPT_CC_OUT` records and `CC_MAX_TURNS` is unenforced. Both live in the shared `run_3arm.sh` path and deserve a coordinated change, not a drive-by from me at the end of a long session.

**One correction to my own commit.** My first graphmark commit message claimed to add the scorers, but `agentic-swebench/logs` is gitignored so only `collect_patch.sh` landed. I caught it before pushing, moved them to the tracked `analysis/` tree, and amended — the pushed commit matches its message.

        inst=os.path.basename(idir.rstrip("/")); f=idir+"cc_out.json"; p=idir+"patch.diff"
        if not os.path.exists(f): drops[f"{arm}:no_cc_out"]+=1; continue
        raw=open(f,errors="ignore").read()
        if "CORRUPT_CC_OUT" in raw: drops[f"{arm}:CORRUPT_CC_OUT"]+=1; continue
        try: J=json.loads(raw)
        except Exception: drops[f"{arm}:unparseable"]+=1; continue
        if isinstance(J,list): J=J[0] if J else {}
        if J.get("subtype")!="success": drops[f"{arm}:subtype={J.get('subtype')}"]+=1; continue
        if J.get("is_error"): drops[f"{arm}:is_error"]+=1; continue
        if not(os.path.exists(p) and os.path.getsize(p)>0): drops[f"{arm}:empty_patch"]+=1; continue
        rec[(arm,inst)]={"cost":J.get("total_cost_usd") or 0,"tok":usage_total(J),
                         "turns":J.get("num_turns") or 0,"ms":J.get("duration_ms") or 0}
# ---------- transcripts -> calls
calls=collections.defaultdict(lambda:{"tot":0,"graph":0})
for arm in ("eg","baseline"):
    for f in glob.glob(f"{S}/results/{TAG}_r1_{arm}/ccfg/projects/*/*.jsonl"):
        inst=None; tot=0; g=0
        for ln in open(f,errors="ignore"):
            ln=ln.strip()
            if not ln or ln[0]!="{": continue
            try: r=json.loads(ln)
            except Exception: continue
            if inst is None and r.get("cwd"): inst=os.path.basename(r["cwd"])
            if r.get("type")!="assistant": continue
            c=(r.get("message") or {}).get("content")
            if not isinstance(c,list): continue
            for b in c:
                if isinstance(b,dict) and b.get("type")=="tool_use":
                    tot+=1
                    if is_graph(b.get("name",""),b.get("input") or {}): g+=1
        if inst: calls[(arm,inst)]["tot"]+=tot; calls[(arm,inst)]["graph"]+=g
# ---------- pair
pairs=[]
for (arm,inst),v in rec.items():
    if arm!="eg": continue
    b=rec.get(("baseline",inst))
    if not b: continue
    pairs.append({"inst":inst,"e":v,"b":b,
                  "ce":calls.get(("eg",inst),{"tot":0,"graph":0}),
                  "cb":calls.get(("baseline",inst),{"tot":0,"graph":0})})
print(f"=== {TAG} — prereg d096913c166b5ebe ===")
print(f"  gated pairs: {len(pairs)}   (prereg requires >= 35)")
if drops:
    print("  drops:")
    for k,v in sorted(drops.items(),key=lambda kv:-kv[1]): print(f"    {k:34} {v}")
if len(pairs)<5:
    print("  too few pairs to score"); raise SystemExit
# ---------- PRIMARY: substitution ratio
gp=[p for p in pairs if p["ce"]["graph"]>0 and p["ce"]["tot"]>0 and p["cb"]["tot"]>0]
if gp:
    G=sum(p["ce"]["graph"] for p in gp)/len(gp)
    E=sum(p["ce"]["tot"] for p in gp)/len(gp)
    B=sum(p["cb"]["tot"] for p in gp)/len(gp)
    disp=(B-E)+G
    print(f"\n=== PRIMARY: substitution ratio (n={len(gp)} with transcripts) ===")
    print(f"  eg calls/session        {E:6.2f}")
    print(f"  baseline calls/session  {B:6.2f}")
    print(f"  graph calls/session     {G:6.2f}")
    print(f"  calls displaced         {disp:+6.2f}")
    print(f"  RATIO                   {disp/G:6.3f}   (Opus reference 0.980; prereg predicts > 1.10)")
    print(f"  VERDICT: {'PASS - exceeds 1.10' if disp/G>1.10 else 'FAIL - 1:1 substitution holds, model-independent'}")
else:
    print("\n  PRIMARY unavailable: no transcripts parsed")
# ---------- SECONDARY: tokens & cost
def boot(vals,it=5000):
    rnd=random.Random(20260811); out=[]
    for _ in range(it):
        s=[vals[rnd.randrange(len(vals))] for _ in range(len(vals))]
        num=sum(b for _,b in s); den=sum(a for a,_ in s)
        out.append((num-den)/num if num else 0)
    out.sort(); return out[int(.025*it)],out[int(.975*it)]
print(f"\n=== SECONDARY: savings (n={len(pairs)}) ===")
for k,lab,ref in (("tok","tokens","+6.22%"),("cost","cost","+4.61%")):
    ve=[p["e"][k] for p in pairs]; vb=[p["b"][k] for p in pairs]

    per=[(b-e)/b for e,b in zip(ve,vb) if b]
    lo,hi=boot(list(zip(ve,vb)))

# ---------- wall clock + turns
print(f"\n=== WALL-CLOCK and TURNS (report beside tokens, per prereg) ===")
for k,lab,unit in (("ms","wall-clock","min"),("turns","turns","")):
    e=sum(p["e"][k] for p in pairs); b=sum(p["b"][k] for p in pairs)

          + ("   (negative = eg SLOWER)" if k=="ms" else ""))
tot=sum(p["e"]["cost"]+p["b"]["cost"] for p in pairs)
print(f"\n  cell spend on gated pairs: ${tot:.2f}")
PY

All three PRs are up:

| repo | PR | what |
|---|---|---|
| entire-graph | **https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph/pull/92** | search cache stopped dying on a stray `.DS_Store` — 3704ms → 131ms warm |
| entire-graph | **https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph/pull/93** | Go 1.24 → 1.26 across go.mod, mise.toml and CI |
| graphmark | **https://github.com/entirehq/graphmark/pull/70** | patch contamination fix + the 13 analysis scorers |

On the Go bump specifically: I installed 1.26.5 and ran the repo's actual gate rather than just editing pins, because the provider builds tree-sitter through CGO and that's where a toolchain bump usually breaks. Build, vet, gofmt, full tests (`sem` 59.9s) and full **race** tests (`sem` 171.9s) all pass. I flagged one thing in the PR for the reviewer to decide: raising the `go` directive to 1.26 raises the module's minimum toolchain for anything vendoring it as a library, and offered the `toolchain go1.26.5` alternative if they'd rather keep the floor at 1.24.

**HAIKU50 is running clean:** 27/100 done, 20 live, 9 minutes in, **0 fatals, 0 fairness aborts**, roughly 24 minutes to go. All 11 preflight gates passed including the live auth probe I rewrote after the old env-var check gave a false green on this box.

Scoring is already written and installed (`logs/score_haiku50.py`), and a waiter will fire when the run drains. It reports the prereg's endpoints in order — **PRIMARY is the substitution ratio**, not the token number, since a token total at n=50 can't separate a working tool from a baseline that flailed. Prediction sealed in advance: ratio above 1.10 (Opus measured 0.980) and tokens +10% to +25% (Opus +6.22%), on the theory that a weaker model flails more and so leaves more displaceable work. If the ratio stays near 1.0, the 1:1-substitute finding is model-independent and the token number is noise whatever it says. Wall-clock goes beside it, since eg ran 7.9% slower on Opus.

Interim read — **and I need to caveat this hard, because I've been burned by exactly this before.** At 15 of 50 pairs:

```
tokens   pooled  -3.84%   median +0.22%   equal-wt  -8.21%   CI [-20.36,+9.63]   wins  8/15
cost     pooled  +2.30%   median +6.20%   equal-wt  -0.64%   CI [ -9.64,+11.60]  wins 10/15
                                                              Opus ref: tokens +6.22%, cost +4.61%

PRIMARY  eg calls 67.14  baseline 61.29  graph 4.29  ->  displaced -1.57, RATIO -0.367
wall-clock  eg 7.59min vs baseline 7.50min (-1.27%, eg slower)
turns       eg 59.47 vs baseline 56.80
```

**Why you should not trust these numbers yet.** They come from the pairs that finished *first*, and I measured that bias directly in an earlier cell: finished-first pairs are significantly cheaper, permutation p=0.0052. A partial ratio here read +76% on a cell that was nothing like that when complete. Also 18 of 33 records dropped as unparseable (13 baseline, 5 eg) — those are files still being written mid-run, not defects, but the asymmetry alone can swing a 15-pair read.

**What is nonetheless worth noting.** The direction is against my sealed prediction, not for it. I predicted the substitution ratio would exceed 1.10 on a weaker model because Haiku should flail more and leave more displaceable work. Instead eg is making **more** calls than baseline (67.1 vs 61.3), so the ratio is negative — the graph is adding work rather than displacing it. If that holds at n=50, the 1:1-substitute finding is not just model-independent, it's worse on Haiku, and the token number is noise whatever it lands on.

Two other early signals: Haiku is hitting the 120-turn cap (`error_max_turns` on 2 baselines), and eg is again slightly slower in wall-clock, consistent with Opus.

On fairness, I checked the thing I flagged about load: `run_paired.sh` **alternates arm order per instance** (`_order=(eg baseline)` on even indices, reversed on odd), so the cold-start penalty and the 20-wide contention land on both arms roughly equally instead of becoming a per-cell offset. That was the specific risk at load 20 on a 32-core box, and the harness already controls for it.

~15 minutes left. I'll score the full set when it drains and report against the prereg rather than this partial.

content.text:
**The 28x** is the index-build phase on a repeat search, from PR #92's measurement:

```
run 1: cache_hit=False  index_ms=3704   total_ms=4480
run 2: cache_hit=True   index_ms=131    total_ms=908
run 3: cache_hit=True   index_ms=126    total_ms=887
```

3704 → 131 ms is 28x. Here's what's actually happening. Every `entire graph search` has to have an index of the repo's symbols and relations. Building that from scratch on entire-graph costs ~3.7 seconds. There's a cache keyed on the git tree hash, so a second search should read it back in ~130 ms instead of rebuilding.

The bug was that the cache was gated on the working tree being *completely* pristine — `git status --porcelain --untracked-files=all` compared against empty output. A single `.DS_Store` made that non-empty, so the gate said "dirty, don't cache," and **every** search rebuilt the whole index. On the real checkout I measured `index_cache_hit=false` with `index_latency_ms=9062` on back-to-back identical queries.

Three honest qualifications on that number:

- **It's the index phase, not the whole command.** Total latency went 4480 → 887 ms, so the user-visible win is **5x**, not 28x. The remainder is query work and process startup, which no cache helps.
- **It only helps warm repeats.** The first search still pays 3704 ms; a cache can't help a cold run. Since the graph gets called ~2.71 times per session, roughly 1.7 of those calls benefit.
- **It only fires when every dirty path is unindexable.** An untracked `.go` or `.md` correctly still defeats the cache. My own entire-graph checkout has untracked `.md` plan files, and markdown *is* indexed, so the fix wouldn't fully help there. It targets `.DS_Store`, compiled binaries, logs, editor swap files — which is what's usually lying around.

Why I bothered: it's the one concrete lever on the finding that eg runs **7.9% slower in wall-clock** than no-tool, which nobody had measured before today and which a user actually feels.

Now, the grading — I've hit a real blocker you should know before the lid closes:

```
results/ is 543G, only 116G free (89% used)
swebench python package: NOT installed
grade_pairs.sh: hardcoded to the Mac (stale scratchpad path + Mac docker socket)
docker: up, 1.26GB reclaimable
REP30F patches on disk: eg 29, baseline 30

On the **best fair rep50 run, about 4.2 million tokens.** Here are the rep50-family cells with absolute deltas:

```
cell         n   tokens saved      pct     status
R50FIX      48    +28,729,721   16.11%    WITHDRAWN - in-sample

CS50B       45    +15,160,669    9.99%    same in-sample family

REP50X      48     +4,110,559    2.90%    FAIR, representative draw

GUIDE50     50     -4,077,292   -9.79%    fair, negative
HAIKU50     46     -9,761,921   -5.86%    fair, negative (today)
```

So the answer depends entirely on which number you're allowed to quote:

**The honest one: +4.2M tokens (HOLD50) or +4.1M (REP50X)** — the two fair, out-of-sample rep50 cells, landing at 2.2% and 2.9%. Pool them and it's ~8.3M tokens across 96 pairs.

**The big one, +28.7M at 16.11% (R50FIX), is withdrawn** — it was in-sample, and when the same config ran on a representative draw it gave +2.89%, not +16.10%. The gap came from that cell's *baseline* flailing (62.2 → 52.9 turns), not from eg improving.

**CS50's +20.1M is also withdrawn** for a different reason: it scored +12.86% while its `locate_symbol` calls *rose*, which is the mechanism moving backwards. A token win with the mechanism going the wrong way is baseline drift, not a tool effect.

One cell worth mentioning even though it isn't rep50: **REP30F at +7.0M / 7.87%** is the best *verified*-fair result on the board (30/30 prompt digests matched, out-of-sample) — which is exactly why I pointed the grading run at it rather than at a bigger-looking number.

So if you want a single defensible sentence: *on a fair, out-of-sample rep50, entire-graph saved on the order of 4 million tokens out of ~150–200M, i.e. 2–3%.* The 28M figure exists but can't be used.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Grades REP30F both arms. Partitions predictions across the TWO datasets the suite
# draws from (SWE-bench_Multilingual + SWE-bench_Verified) -- the first attempt failed

# 1. partition every arm's predictions by dataset membership
python3 - >> "$L" 2>&1 <<'"'"'PY'"'"'
import json,os,glob
from datasets import load_dataset
S=os.path.expanduser("~/pe1/graphmark/agentic-swebench")
sets={}
for name,short in (("swe-bench/SWE-bench_Multilingual","ML"),("princeton-nlp/SWE-bench_Verified","VER")):

    for short,(name,ids) in sets.items():
        sub=[x for x in preds if x["instance_id"] in ids]
        if not sub: continue
        f=f"{S}/preds_{tag}_{short}.json"

Grading finished. Here's the full state of everything running:

**Correctness (the measurement never run before today)**
```
REP30F, 30 instances attempted per arm
             attempted   patch   RESOLVED    rate
eg                30       29       29      96.7%
baseline          30       30       30     100.0%

The graph did not improve correctness — it cost one instance (`redis__redis-10095`: reported success at 24 turns, produced an empty patch). More importantly, **baseline resolves 30/30, so this suite has no correctness headroom at all.** No tool can show a resolution gain against a ceiling. That closes my own second thought honestly: I was right that correctness was never measured, wrong that measuring it would rescue anything.

I verified the grading was real rather than a no-op — `apache__lucene-13170` shows 719 lines of Gradle output, BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 2m29s, 244 tasks executed, FAIL_TO_PASS 1/1 and PASS_TO_PASS 8/8.

**Housekeeping done** — disk reclaimed 116G → **659G**, credential file deleted from the VM, three PRs open (#92, #93, graphmark #70).

Two things I got wrong along the way and had to fix, worth recording since they'd bite anyone repeating this:

- I graded against `SWE-bench_Verified` alone. The suite draws from **two** datasets — 26 of 30 instances are Multilingual (lucene, carbon, caddy, ruff), only 3 are Verified. Predictions have to be partitioned by dataset membership.
- I nearly reported **29/29 = 100%** for eg. That's `resolved/submitted`, which flatters the tool by hiding the instance where it produced no patch. The honest denominator is `resolved/attempted` = 96.7%.

So the complete picture from today: on a fair, out-of-sample rep50 the graph saves roughly **4 million tokens out of ~150–200M (2–3%)**, runs **7.9% slower** in wall-clock, is **worse on a cheaper model** (ratio 0.436 vs 0.980), and **cannot be shown to improve correctness** because the benchmark is saturated. The mechanism behind all of it is that it displaces 0.980 calls per call it makes.

Still on you: **rotate that token.**

baseline          27/27    3/3     30/30       30         100.0%

**Result: no correctness benefit. The graph came out one instance behind.**

The single eg loss is `redis__redis-10095` — the session reported `subtype=success` after 24 turns but produced an empty patch, so the agent finished without editing anything. One instance at n=30 carries no statistical weight, but the direction is negative rather than positive.

The finding that matters more than the 3.3-point gap: **baseline resolves 30 of 30.** The suite is saturated, so there is no correctness headroom for any tool to win. That makes "measure correctness instead of tokens" unmeasurable here rather than unfavourable — and it explains why this campaign was structurally forced onto token savings from the start.

I checked the grading was genuine rather than a silent no-op, because a 100% rate is exactly the shape a broken evaluation produces: `apache__lucene-13170` has 719 lines of real Gradle output, `BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 2m 29s`, 244 tasks executed, FAIL_TO_PASS 1/1 and PASS_TO_PASS 8/8.

input.command:
cat > /tmp/mac_move_bench.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Move benchmark data off the Mac: tar -> upload to GCS -> VERIFY -> delete local.
# Nothing is deleted until its object is confirmed present with a non-zero size.
L=$HOME/mac_move_bench.log
B=gs://graphmark-evidence-504800/mac-offload-20260812
say(){ echo "[$(date +%H:%M:%S)] $*" >> "$L"; }
free(){ df -g / | awk 'NR==2{print $4}'; }
say "START free=$(free)GiB"

move(){  # $1=path  $2=label
  local p="$1" lbl="$2"
  [ -e "$p" ] || { say "$lbl: absent, skip"; return; }
  local sz; sz=$(du -sh "$p" 2>/dev/null | cut -f1)
  say "$lbl ($sz): tarring"
  tar -czf "/tmp/${lbl}.tgz" -C "$(dirname "$p")" "$(basename "$p")" 2>>"$L"
  local tsz; tsz=$(stat -f%z "/tmp/${lbl}.tgz" 2>/dev/null)
  say "$lbl: tarball ${tsz} bytes, uploading"
  if ! gcloud storage cp "/tmp/${lbl}.tgz" "$B/${lbl}.tgz" >>"$L" 2>&1; then
    say "$lbl: UPLOAD FAILED -- keeping local copy"; rm -f "/tmp/${lbl}.tgz"; return
  fi
  # verify: object exists AND size matches
  local rsz; rsz=$(gcloud storage ls -l "$B/${lbl}.tgz" 2>/dev/null | awk 'NR==1{print $1}')
  if [ "$rsz" = "$tsz" ] && [ -n "$rsz" ]; then
    say "$lbl: VERIFIED in GCS ($rsz bytes) -- deleting local"
    chmod -R u+w "$p" 2>/dev/null
    rm -rf "$p" 2>/dev/null
    rm -f "/tmp/${lbl}.tgz"
    say "$lbl: local deleted, free=$(free)GiB"
  else
    say "$lbl: VERIFY MISMATCH local=$tsz remote=$rsz -- keeping local copy"
    rm -f "/tmp/${lbl}.tgz"
  fi
}

## Overview
SWE-Bench Pro introduces a new benchmark for evaluating AI agents on complex, real-world software engineering tasks, featuring contamination-resistant problems sourced from GPL-licensed and proprietary commercial codebases.

## Benchmark Size and Structure
SWE-BENCH PRO contains 1,865 problems sourced from a diverse set of 41 actively maintained repositories spanning business applications, B2B services, and developer tools.

The benchmark is partitioned into a public set with open access to problems sourced from 11 repositories, a held-out set of 12 repositories and a commercial set of 18 proprietary repositories where we have formal partnership agreements with early-stage startups.

## Long-Horizon Tasks
The benchmark features long-horizon tasks that may require hours to days for a professional software engineer to complete, often involving patches across multiple files and substantial code modifications.

## Resolution Rates
Current frontier models achieved resolve rates below 45% on public tasks and less than 20% on commercial tasks, indicating a significant gap in autonomous software development capabilities.

## Contamination Resistance
The approach involves exclusively selecting repositories distributed under strong copyleft licenses (GPL) to construct a public set (11 repositories) and a held-out set (12 repositories), and acquiring commercial codebases from real startups to capture enterprise-grade problems in a commercial set (18 repositories).

All tasks are human-verified and augmented with sufficient context to ensure resolvability.

## Overview

SWE-EVO is a benchmark for long-horizon software evolution, constructed from release notes of seven mature open-source Python projects. It comprises 48 tasks requiring multi-step modifications spanning an average of 21 files, validated against test suites averaging 874 tests per instance.

Unlike SWE-Bench's focus on individual issues, SWE-EVO defines tasks as the evolution from one tagged release version to the next, using release notes as the specification for required changes.

SWE-EVO tasks involve significantly longer natural-language specifications (average 2390.5 words vs. SWE-Bench's shorter issue descriptions), require modifications across a much broader scope (average 20.9 files edited in gold patches), and involve larger test suites (average 874 total tests).

Here's the answer, and one piece of arithmetic in it cuts against the obvious choice.

## Recommendation: SWE-bench Pro (public set), with SWE-EVO as the mechanism cell

**[SWE-bench Pro](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.16941)** hits every condition I measured:

| my win condition | SWE-bench Pro |
|---|---|
| long baseline sessions (74% win rate at 69–136 calls) | tasks take a professional engineer **hours to days** |
| cross-file changes (where `callers`/`impact` pay) | patches span **multiple files**, substantial modifications |
| uncontaminated repos (so localization is genuinely hard) | GPL + **18 proprietary commercial** repos, contamination-resistant by construction |
| correctness headroom | **<45% public, <20% commercial** — versus our suite's saturated 100% |
| enough n for power | **1,865 problems / 41 repos** |

That last row matters: our REP30F cell had baseline resolving 30/30, so no tool could show a correctness gain. Here the baseline fails most of the time, which is where a locator earns its keep.

**[SWE-EVO](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.18470v5)** is the purer test of the mechanism but too small to headline: **48 tasks, average 20.9 files edited per gold patch**, 874 tests, 2,390-word specs, and only 25% resolution for GPT-5.4/OpenHands versus 72.8% on SWE-bench Verified. A 21-file patch is exactly what `RELATED SITES` and `impact` exist for — I measured that label at only 10.1% precision on single-hunk SWE-bench patches, and on a 21-file change the base rate of genuinely-related files is far higher. But at n=48 my MDE is around 25 points, so it can demonstrate the mechanism, not carry the number.

I'm ruling out **[NL2Repo-Bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.12730)** despite it being the most fashionable long-horizon option: it starts from an **empty workspace**, so there is no existing code to locate and the graph has literally nothing to index.

## The arithmetic, including the part that hurts

For 25% cost savings on `cost ≈ turns^1.179`, eg must use **21.7% fewer turns**. In my winning bin I measured eg 73.0 vs baseline 85.0 — only 14.1% fewer, giving +17.9%. To close that at B=85 the substitution ratio must reach **~7.95**; I measured **5.53**.

And here's the uncomfortable bit: **graph calls stayed flat at ~2.65–2.71 per session regardless of difficulty** (winners vs losers, p=0.91). If that holds on longer tasks, then as sessions grow the *absolute* displacement needed grows while the graph's call budget doesn't — so the percentage saving would **shrink**, not grow. Longer tasks only help if the ratio keeps climbing, i.e. each call prevents more flailing. It rose from −0.09 to +5.53 across my observed range, so reaching ~8 is a modest extrapolation — but it is an extrapolation, and extrapolating past the measured range is exactly what produced five withdrawn headlines here.

## Two traps to pre-register against before spending

**Selection on the gate.** With baselines failing >55%, the both-arms-succeed gate will drop most pairs, and survivors are non-random. Worse, failed baselines hit `max_turns`, which inflates baseline turns and manufactures eg savings. I'd pre-register the resolved-rate denominator as *attempted*, not *submitted* — the same error that nearly had me report 100% instead of 96.7% today.

**Repo-scale cost.** These are large proprietary codebases; the graph index build was already 3.7–9.1s on entire-graph, and that's the wall-clock tax that made eg 7.9% slower. PR #92 helps; it may not be enough.

The honest framing: this is the first benchmark I've seen where the win condition and the task shape actually line up, and I'd put the prediction at **+15% to +25%** with the mechanism endpoint (substitution ratio ≥ 7.9) as the thing that decides it — not the token total.
