I've sent Codex the review it asked for of the combined candidate (#292): how the accuracy fix interacts with caching and with #290's safety checks. I read the source only, with no builds or runs.

**Cleared, with evidence:**
- Cached queries never store word-count statistics; they're recalculated on every search.
- #290's "quarantine" of suspicious output lines happens after ranking, so it can't affect the counts.
- A cancelled search can't be recorded as having exact statistics.
- Multi-pass file selection doesn't read any file twice, so nothing is double-counted.

**Worth knowing (existing behaviour, not caused by this fix):** the saved-answer replay doesn't record which version of the tool produced a result. If a task spans a tool upgrade, it can replay the old ranking.

**Open issue (a hypothesis I haven't tested):** since the fix that makes unreadable files cancel exact statistics, even one tracked file over 4 MiB can cancel them on the uncached path. The file doesn't need to contain any query word.
- The cached Git path doesn't read files that don't match, so it keeps exact statistics. The two paths would then disagree.
- The fix would also do nothing on the uncached path in repos with large generated files, which is common.
- The earlier fresh-case improvement was measured before this rule existed, so it may not hold on such repos.
- One test repo, fx-graph, has 10 files over 4 MiB (generated parsers), though its ignore rules may exclude them.
- I proposed a minimal test and two possible fixes. Nothing is coded until Codex agrees.

**Old benchmark files:** I gave Codex the exact, limited command to list the storage bucket, but haven't run it. gcloud's login here has expired, so you'd need to run `gcloud auth login` first.

I've sent Codex my review of its fix for the wrong test command. The fix stops a Python file in a Go repo from being told to run `go test`, but it breaks some Go cases, and other languages can still make the same mistake. I only read the code and ran nothing.

**It breaks Go files that don't end in `.go`.** The fix only accepts `.go` files, but these other Go package files are also checked by `go test`:
- templates or SQL embedded into Go code;
- C files compiled into Go (cgo) and Go assembly files (`.s`);
- `testdata` golden files that tests compare against.

These used to get the right `go test ./pkg` command. Now they get nothing, or another language's command. I suggested treating a file as Go when its folder contains Go code, not only when it ends in `.go`.

**Other languages can still win wrongly.** The tool walks up from the edited file and, at each folder, tries languages in a fixed order (Rust first). The first match wins.
- **Same-folder example:** a repo root with both `Cargo.toml` and `pyproject.toml` (common for Rust-backed Python projects) gives `cargo test` for a Python edit.
- **Nearer-folder example:** a `package.json` used only for linting, sitting closer to a Python file, gives `npm test` even though the project's pytest config is higher up.

I proposed one rule for all languages:
- Only a language that owns the file can match, and the tool looks all the way up for one.
- General tools like `make` are tried only if no language matched anywhere.
- A script that explicitly calls another language's test tool (`"test": "pytest"`) is still honoured.
- I listed the tests that would prove each case.

- **#292:** unaffected, since this fix is on a separate branch. It is still fully green and only needs your approval.

Codex found a more serious harness bug and fixed it in **draft GraphMark #86**, stacked on #85.

- **The bug:** two benchmark runs executing at the same time share one generated `gq` wrapper. When run B rewrites that wrapper, run A's graph queries start searching **B's repository**. Codex reproduced it in both tool modes.

- **The fix:** each run now gets its own wrapper and its own writable search cache.

MODELS="${MODELS:-haiku sonnet opus}"
ARMS="${ARMS:-baseline treated}"
case "$CONC" in ''|*[!0-9]*) echo 'CONC must be a positive integer' >&2; exit 2;; esac

# Fixed-budget terminality evidence — 2026-09-28

This is follow-up policy evidence, not a change to Task1's normal-return-only
provider schema, and not verification of the locally installed Claude version.
No model, auth command, package installation or experiment was run.

## Primary sources checked

- [Claude Code CLI reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference)
  explicitly distinguishes the print-mode turn cap from ordinary completion:
  reaching the configured cap exits with an error. Thus nonzero process status
  alone cannot distinguish an intended trial boundary from an unplanned harness
  or provider failure.
- [Anthropic's scheduled reviewer recipe](https://platform.claude.com/cookbook/claude-agent-sdk-scheduled-repository-reviewer-scheduled-repository-reviewer)
  documents budget-limited terminal error results and an induced turn-cap example.
  This supports a distinct budget-stop category, but its SDK example is not an
  installed-CLI compatibility test for this worktree.
- [Official Python SDK result types](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-agent-sdk-python/blob/main/src/claude_agent_sdk/types.py)
  distinguish an agent result from the final task-quality judgment and carry
  error/termination metadata. The current types also document API errors whose
  subtype can still be success; the exact error Boolean remains essential.
- [Official Python SDK error handling](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-agent-sdk-python/blob/main/src/claude_agent_sdk/_errors.py)
  preserves terminal-error metadata alongside a nonzero CLI exit. These are
  rolling-source observations, not a pinned supported receipt-version matrix.

## Required before a fixed-budget causal cohort

Separate trial termination, agent protocol outcome and evaluated task resolution.
An explicitly supported normal return or preregistered budget stop must freeze
the attempt; neither empty patches nor unavailable accounting authorize a rerun.
Collection, cleanup, expected identity and artifact integrity remain mandatory.

Turn-cap support needs a pinned receipt schema/version and regression evidence;
unknown or inconsistent payloads stay unsupported. Launcher wall-stop support
needs positive deadline and process-cessation evidence, not a truncated receipt
or the assumption that killing one PID killed every descendant. Process-group
cleanup alone is not adversarial proof against detached descendants; do not
make a hermeticity or universal process-tree claim from synthetic group tests.

Observed costs remain separate from usability of token/cost comparisons. A
quality-eligible capped patch may still lack complete accounting, which blocks
a savings decision rather than inventing zero spend.

This policy must be designed and verified before claiming the repaired harness
supports a complete fixed-budget experiment. Task1 currently conservatively
refuses capped/error results while preserving the occupied slot; it must not be
marketed as the finished trial-terminal protocol.

Codex asked what the installed Claude Code (2.1.283) records when a run stops at its turn limit, so the benchmark can file that as a deliberate budget stop rather than a failure to retry. I found the answer in public publisher-authored files for that exact version, without running Claude or reading any sessions, and sent it to Codex.

**How the version link was pinned:**
- The installed binary's path shows version **2.1.283**. It's a compiled build, so its format can't be read without scanning the binary, which Codex ruled out.
- The public npm package for 2.1.283 only documents tool inputs and outputs, not the result format.
- The companion Agent SDK `0.3.283` declares in its npm metadata that it bundles **Claude Code 2.1.283**. That's the publisher's own link to the exact installed version. I saved its type file to the scratchpad and recorded its hash.

**What that version records when a run ends:**
- A turn-limit stop has `subtype: "error_max_turns"`. There's also an optional `terminal_reason: "max_turns"`, which may be missing.
- `is_error` is a plain true/false field, not fixed for any outcome. A `"success"` result with `is_error: true` means the run ended on an API error, not a normal finish. So classification must use `subtype`, never `is_error` alone.

**Limits I told Codex:**
- These are the SDK's type definitions, not a captured sample of real CLI output, so they don't prove real output matches byte for byte.
- Nothing pins the exit code for a turn-limit stop. It should only back up the classification, not decide it.
- Three other Claude Code versions are installed, so each run's record must note which version produced it.

My recommendation: classify results by `subtype`, tied to 2.1.283, and reject results from any other version until each is pinned the same way.

## What

The session echo (`EG_SEARCH_SESSION`) replays the first query's rendered payload (its ranking, snippets and budget) under a header saying the question was not run again. The replay identity covered repository, tree, corpus-policy fingerprint and output format, **but not the binary that rendered it**. A task whose session spans a binary upgrade was therefore served the old binary's ranking.

The scope now carries a **producer identity**: version plus the VCS revision Go stamps into the binary, with a `+modified` marker when the binary was built from a modified tree. A state file without a producer matches nothing, so it falls back to a real search, the same rule the other identity fields already follow. No schema bump is needed; that avoids a conflict with #290, which moves the schema to 3.

## A bug caught on the way

The producer is set **inside `searchSessionScopeFor`**, not at call sites. The replay decision rebuilds the scope twice after its policy checks. A first draft set the producer at only one of those three sites, and every replay was silently refused. The existing replay tests caught it.

- `TestSearchSessionProducerRefusesAnUnidentifiableBinary` checks that a binary with neither version nor revision gets no identity.
- One existing fixture was updated to include the new identity field, so it still describes "same scope".

## Known limit

Two builds from **differently modified** trees at the same revision share an identity. That is development-only. Refusing every modified build instead would disable replay for all local builds and make behaviour depend on whether the checkout is dirty.

Not merging.

content.text:
I opened **entire-graph #294**. It stops a saved search from being replayed after the tool is upgraded, which could hand an agent results ranked by the old version.

- **The bug:** within one task, the session feature can repeat the first search's saved output instead of searching again. Its record noted the repo, the code version, the settings and the output format, but not which tool build produced the saved output.
- **The fix:** the record now includes the tool's version and the Git revision it was built from, flagged if built from uncommitted changes. A record saved before this change is ignored, and a fresh search runs.
- **A mistake I caught:** the replay check builds that record in three places, and my first version set the new field in only one. That silently disabled all replays; the existing tests flagged it. I moved the field into the one shared builder, and added the lesson to my memory notes.
- **Tests:** all 22 session tests pass, run one at a time at low priority. The new test fails if the version check is removed. A same-version control confirms replay still works when it should.
- **Known limit:** two builds made from differently edited copies of the same revision count as the same build. That only affects local development.

I've told Codex. #294 touches the same file as #290, so it may need a small rebase if #292 merges first.

The rest is unchanged and waiting on you: approving the pull requests (#292 and #293 need marking "ready" first), and your pending decisions.

I'm working on the biggest gap left in the goal: search that understands meaning, not just matching words. Right now the graph misses code when the query is worded differently from the code's own comments.

**Done so far:**
- **Pass/fail rules:** written down and hashed before I've seen any reworded query or result.
  - I'll develop on reworded versions of the 40 diagnosis cases, and evaluate once on reworded versions of the 40 fresh ones.
  - A fix fails if it finds no more targets in the top 10 than the current versions, if it drops a case they had in the top 3 out of the top 10, or if it hurts the normal-wording results.
- **Test runner:** ready. It runs one search at a time at low priority and can resume after an interruption.
- **Rewordings:** a Sonnet agent is writing one reworded query per case (80 total), describing what each function does without reusing any of its comment or name words. It checks that rule with a script, and I'll re-check it myself.

**Next:** measure how the current versions do on reworded queries. Then try the cheapest fix first: a list of synonyms for common code concepts, fed through the existing abbreviation system so "remove" also matches "delete".

**How the graph has improved so far.** None of this is merged yet: every change is an open PR, and all figures are offline replays of individual searches, not measured agent sessions.

**1. Tokens: search output is 2.6× smaller (#275)**
- The guide now tells agents to use the compact agent output instead of JSON.
- On 40 real code-finding queries, the median response fell from **17,544 → 6,714 bytes**.
- The results are identical: same targets found, same ranks.

**2. Accuracy: finding the right code (#291, bundled in #292)**
- I found why the graph lost to grep. It judged how rare each query word was using only the few files it had pre-picked, so the one rare word that identifies the target counted for almost nothing. It now uses the whole repo.
- 40 fresh cases, never used to find the bug, with the pass/fail rules written down in advance:

  | | found in top 10 | top 3 | rank 1 |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | before | 30 | 25 | 13 |
  | after | **38** | **33** | 14 |

  14 cases got better and none got worse.
- The 40 cases used to find the bug went from 26 → 33 in the top 3. That set is in-sample, so it counts for less than the fresh one.
- 34 real bug-fix tasks were essentially unchanged: 25 → 26 in the top 5, with one case better and one worse.
- Results are now the same whether or not a cached index was used.

**3. Correct test commands the graph tells agents to run (#288, #293)**
- It no longer picks a runner just because the word appears somewhere. For example, it won't suggest `npx jest` for a Playwright project, or `pytest` because a comment mentions it.
- An escaped quote in a script no longer hides the real test command.
- It no longer tells agents to run `go test` on Python files in a mixed repo, while Go-adjacent C and assembly files are still handled correctly.

**4. Smaller correctness fixes**
- A saved search can't be replayed after the tool is upgraded (#294).
- A flaky statusline test is fixed (#286).
- When space is tight, the top result keeps its rank, name and score instead of shrinking to a bare file path (#289).

**5. Trustworthy benchmark numbers (GraphMark #83–#88, mostly Codex's work)** Each of these could quietly distort results:
- failed runs reported as successes;
- concurrent runs searching each other's repository;
- retries overwriting earlier results;
- partial token counts treated as full ones.

**What didn't work, and what's still open**
- The first version of #289 cut output size by 57%, but only by dropping the full code for results ranked 2–5, where 12 of the 40 targets were. Keeping the top 5 whole only saves about 8%, so the 2.6× from #275 is essentially the whole output-size win.
- **Reworded queries still miss.** When a query doesn't use the code's own words, the graph fails. That's the gap I'm working on now.
- **There's no measurement yet that whole agent sessions use fewer tokens or succeed more often.** That needs a paid comparison.

# PR294 independent replay-identity review

**Goal:** Task-scoped rendered search replay must be invalidated by a producer version/revision change, retain replay for an identifiable unchanged producer, fail safely for absent/ambiguous identity, and preserve existing replay safety gates.

**Range:** `f22e6c952f3b375261942e6a17af67ca6b1d2e39..f3a67f136268ca68d1077273d92c9e6eacf32f94`.

**Method:** Read-only source review of the exact diff and focused source in `internal/cli/search.go`, `search_session.go`, and `search_session_test.go`; additionally inspected the coordinator-authorized `internal/cli/root.go:22-46` and `cmd/entire-graph/main.go:15-18` to trace version defaulting. Compared the base revision's decoder/state/matcher contract directly. Used the requesting-code-review checklist and impl-validator protocol. No tests, builds, providers, graph/brain engines, network, private sessions, or other agents were executed. This report is the only file written; source/index/HEAD were not changed.

## Strengths

- Producer is constructed centrally and supplied at all three scope observations (`search.go:169`, `219`, `237`, `379-380`), including the last pre-output check. Recording copies that scope (`search.go:335`) and persists Producer (`search_session.go:283`). The unchanged-producer positive-control test would catch forgetting one of those three observations.
- New-reader matching requires both producer values to be nonempty and equal (`search_session.go:134-136`); old records without the new field are rejected by the new reader.
- Schema, policy fingerprint, format, repository, tree, and path checks remain conjunctive. Producer does not replace or bypass them. Mutable-worktree exclusion, aggregate-format exclusion, path admission, and terminal-safe output are retained.
- For metadata the helper actually receives, different versions, different nonempty revisions, and clean-versus-modified transitions produce different identities. Identical stable inputs remain eligible for replay.

## Findings

### Important / P2 / FAIL: Missing version becomes a replayable generic producer before the new check

**Location:** `internal/cli/search_session.go:355-358`; caller evidence `internal/cli/root.go:43-46` and `internal/cli/search.go:169`; test gap `internal/cli/search_session_test.go:1008-1016`.

The helper refuses identity only when both version and revision are empty, but the public `Run` entry point replaces an empty version with `"dev"` before dispatch. The executable also defaults its version to `"dev"` (`cmd/entire-graph/main.go:15`). When build information has no VCS revision, the helper therefore returns `"dev+"`, not an empty identity. Two revisionless development binaries from different source revisions share this identity and can replay one another's rendered output. The fallback is a concrete ordinary call path, not a fabricated producer string.

The new unidentifiable-binary test bypasses `Run` and invokes `searchSessionProducer("")` directly, so its success would not establish fail-safe missing-version behavior in the CLI. All existing shared session helpers supply `Version: "0.1.0"` (`search_session_test.go:57-60`), which also hides this path.

**Smallest fix:** Reject the generic development label when revision is absent (or preserve an explicitly separate producer version rather than treating the display fallback as identity). An actual stamped revision may still identify a versionless development build. Keep explicitly identified release builds and stamped development builds eligible according to the intended identity policy.

**Suggested regression, not executed:** In the normal unstamped Go test binary, create a committed synthetic repository and one session path; call `Run` twice with `Options.Version == ""`, `--head`, and two distinct fixture queries. Assert both searches run live and the second returns its own fixture without the replay header. Repeat for explicit `"dev"`; keep the existing named-version same-producer control. A pure helper taking supplied build metadata would make the revisionless premise deterministic instead of relying on the test binary's build information.

### Important / P2 / FAIL: Unchanged replay schema lets pre-PR294 binaries ignore the producer on downgrade

**Location:** new persisted field at `internal/cli/search_session.go:83-84` / `283`, with the unchanged replay schema at `57-61` and assignment at `280`.

PR294 still writes `replay_schema: 2`, exactly the base revision's schema. At the exact base, `searchSessionState` has no Producer field, decoding uses ordinary `json.Unmarshal`, and `matches` checks schema/policy/format/repository/tree without producer (`base search_session.go:69-81`, `119-137`, `233-235`). Thus the old reader silently ignores `producer` and accepts a new writer's otherwise valid schema-2 record. Switching from the PR294 binary back to the base binary can reuse output from the different producer. New-reader rejection of old missing-producer records only protects the opposite direction.

The schema comment explicitly says the schema changes whenever the persisted replay-safety contract changes. This adds such a contract. No security exploit or corpus-policy bypass is claimed: the defect is cross-producer reuse under a still-compatible old safety schema.

**Smallest fix:** Allocate a new replay-schema value for producer-bound records, greater than the schema accepted by supported producer-unaware readers. Coordinate that value with other in-flight schema changes; this review does not claim that choosing 3 independently is sufficient after integration. Keep the nonempty Producer guard for malformed/current-schema states.

**Suggested regression, not executed:** Have the new writer record a replay-eligible HEAD/text response in a synthetic committed fixture. Feed the actual persisted JSON through a legacy schema-2 state decoder/matcher copied narrowly from the exact base and assert refusal. An isolated old-binary/new-binary fixture is stronger if execution is permitted. Also retain a new-reader test rejecting old producer-less records, and a new-writer/new-reader same-producer positive control.

### WARN: Dirty-build identity is the disclosed exception, not a unique binary identity

**Location:** `internal/cli/search_session.go:336-361`.

Two differently modified builds with the same supplied version and stamped VCS revision both get `version+revision+modified`; either can replay the other's response. This limitation is disclosed in the implementation/PR description. Its actual boundary is precise: clean-to-dirty changes invalidate, a stamped revision change invalidates, and a version change invalidates; dirty-A-to-dirty-B at the same version/revision does not. The stamp is build-time metadata, not the current searched repository's dirtiness. It is not accurate to say that merely editing the searched checkout changes the producer or that all local builds lack unique identity.

This is compatible with a narrowly version/revision-based identity policy that intentionally accepts that documented exception, but not with an unconditional promise to refuse every ambiguous producer. The coordinator should explicitly adjudicate that exception. If strict fail-safe ambiguity handling is required, the smallest safe policy is to refuse modified producers; preserving replay for the identical dirty binary needs a stronger stable build identity instead. Refusing modified producers would disable replay for dirty-built binaries, not all clean local builds.

### WARN: New tests establish version changes, but not the other identity dimensions

**Location:** `internal/cli/search_session_test.go:971-1017`.

The integration test has a useful same-version positive control and different-version negative case, with replay-eligible HEAD output. It does not vary stamped revisions or modified status, delete a persisted producer, exercise missing version through `Run`, check an older reader, or assert that a version change resets/re-arms the session for a third call. The helper test relies on actual test-binary build metadata and only checks a version prefix plus the helper's empty case. A regression that removes revision/modified handling while retaining the version string would still satisfy these new tests.

**Smallest improvement:** Isolate producer construction from reading build information and table-test supplied version/revision/modified cases; add the missing-version entry-point regression and legacy-reader regression above. For the version-change integration case, use distinct first/second fixture queries, verify the new Producer was persisted, and verify a third call replays the second payload. These are recommendations from source inspection, not claims that a test was run or failed.

## Checks

| Check | Result | Evidence / limit |
|---|---|---|
| New reader invalidates changed supplied version | PASS | Version included in producer and compared; integration test structure covers it. Source-only. |
| New reader invalidates changed stamped revision | PASS | Revision included in identity. No revision-changing execution/test in this review. |
| Same identifiable producer remains replayable | PASS | All three builders bind Producer; existing and new HEAD positive controls exercise this path structurally. Not executed. |
| No version and no revision fails safely through public entry point | FAIL | `Run` converts empty version to `dev`, producing nonempty `dev+`. |
| Every scope reconstruction binds producer | PASS | Initial, confirmed, final scope all pass `opts.Version`; recording copies scope. |
| New reader refuses missing persisted producer | PASS | Explicit nonempty checks; legacy missing field becomes empty. |
| Older supported reader refuses producer-bound records after downgrade | FAIL | New record retains base schema 2, and base ignores Producer. |
| Modified-build ambiguity is handled according to a clear policy | WARN | Disclosed same-version/same-revision dirty-build alias; requires acceptance or stricter policy. |
| Existing schema/corpus/format/path/output guards remain intact in new reader | PASS | Producer check is additive, and existing downstream checks/sinks remain. |
| New test coverage detects all requested failure modes | WARN | Missing-entry-point, revision, modified, legacy-reader, and re-arm gaps. |
| Runtime tests/builds pass | WARN | Deliberately not executed under delegated execution hold; no runtime verdict offered. |

## Declined to judge

- PR292 patch integration, schema allocation after integration, and token-budget behavior: owned by the coordinator; no duplicate integration check performed.
- Providers, ranking changes, corpus-policy internals, broader repository security, and performance: unchanged/outside the bounded source-review assignment; existing gates were checked only for preserved composition.
- Executed behavior, test pass/fail, and actual release-artifact stamping configuration: execution/network were explicitly prohibited for this reviewer. Metadata-dependent claims above state their conditions.
- Reusing a release version for different unstamped release artifacts, or changes in dependencies/build tags/toolchains at an identical version/revision: not evaluated as additional release-contract defects without the build/release policy in scope.
- Presearch payload replay: separate from the task-scoped session contract under review.

## What

The session echo (`EG_SEARCH_SESSION`) replays the first query's rendered payload (its ranking, snippets and budget) under a header saying the question was not run again. Its identity covered repository, tree, policy and format, **but not the binary that produced it**, so after an upgrade a task could be served the old binary's ranking.

## Policy (revised after independent review of `f3a67f13`)

The producer identity comes **only from the binary's own build metadata**:
- a VCS revision from an **unmodified** tree gives `rev:<revision>`;
- otherwise a real module version (`go install module@version`) gives `mod:<version>`;
- otherwise there is **no identity**, which matches nothing, so the query is answered for real.

The CLI version string is not used, because `Run` turns an empty version into `dev`. Two unstamped dev binaries both reporting `dev` used to replay each other's output. **Modified builds get no identity**: two different modified builds of one revision cannot be told apart.

The replay schema is now **4**, above `main`'s 2 and #292's 3. Producer-unaware readers compare the schema for equality, so after a downgrade they reject these records rather than ignore the producer field. Legacy 2 and 3 records are rejected by this reader.

## Tests

All run serially: 25 session, echo and producer tests pass, with 0 failures and 0 skips.
- A table of producer identities built from build info.
- Control: the same producer still replays.
- A producer change re-arms the session, and a third call replays the *second* payload.
- An empty version and `dev` on unstamped builds, and modified builds, never replay. These are exercised **through `Run`**.
- The persisted record is neither schema 2 nor 3, and legacy 2 and 3 records are rejected.

Build metadata is read through a seam: a test-package default plus a per-call `Options.buildInfo` override. That keeps the tests deterministic regardless of whether the checkout is dirty.

Each defect was shown RED by a mutation that restores it, with the build still compiling:
- schema back to 2;
- modified builds identified;
- `(devel)` accepted as a version.

## Known limits

- A binary built from a modified tree never replays. That is the conservative choice.
- Unstamped release artifacts that share one module version are identified by that version.

Not merging.
EOF

**#294 (the fix that stops an old search result being replayed after the tool changes): third review gap closed.**

"""Fair locate scoring for graph vs embedding. Usage: fair_eval.py <cases.json> <field> <graph_outdir> <label>
Graph: PRIMARY rows only (no section), rank <= 10. Embedding: top-10 symbols by cosine.
Hit (both): same file AND the returned SYMBOL span overlaps the target span.
Records bindings: case-file sha, graph binary sha (from graph dir's BINARY file if present), model digest, cache shas."""
import json,os,sys,hashlib,subprocess,math,re,urllib.request
S="/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-suhaan-devenv/b0108f24-43a4-413e-94c9-bd361b6fafc5/scratchpad"
sys.path.insert(0,S+"/wt-loc/bench/locate"); from doccomment_bench import doc_comment
cases_path,field,gdir,label=sys.argv[1:5]
sha=lambda p: hashlib.sha256(open(p,"rb").read()).hexdigest()
cases=json.load(open(cases_path))
def embed(texts):
    out=[]
    for i in range(0,len(texts),64):
        req=urllib.request.Request("http://localhost:11434/api/embed",data=json.dumps({"model":"nomic-embed-text","input":texts[i:i+64]}).encode(),headers={"Content-Type":"application/json"})
        out+=json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(req,timeout=900))["embeddings"]
    return out
norm=lambda v:(lambda n:[x/n for x in v])(math.sqrt(sum(x*x for x in v)) or 1)
split=lambda n:" ".join(re.sub(r"([a-z0-9])([A-Z])",r"\1 \2",n).replace("_"," ").lower().split())
def index_for(fx):
    cache=f"{S}/embed/{fx}.json"
    if os.path.exists(cache): return json.load(open(cache)),cache
    raw=subprocess.run(["nice","-n","19",S+"/eg-clean","symbols","--repo",f"{S}/{fx}","--format","ndjson"],capture_output=True,text=True,timeout=3600)
    if raw.returncode!=0: raise SystemExit(f"symbols failed for {fx}: rc={raw.returncode}")
    syms=[]
    for line in raw.stdout.splitlines():
        try: d=json.loads(line)
        except Exception: continue
        if d.get("record_type")!="symbol" or d.get("kind") not in ("function","method"): continue
        path=os.path.join(S,fx,d["file_path"])
        doc=doc_comment(path,d["start_line"]) if d.get("language")=="Go" else ""
        try: sig=open(path,errors="ignore").read().splitlines()[d["start_line"]-1].strip()[:200]
        except Exception: sig=""
        syms.append({"file":d["file_path"],"s":d["start_line"],"e":d.get("end_line") or d["start_line"],"text":f"search_document: {split(d.get('name',''))}. {doc} {sig}"[:1500]})
    for x,v in zip(syms,embed([x["text"] for x in syms])): x["v"]=[round(t,5) for t in norm(v)]
    json.dump(syms,open(cache,"w")); print(fx,"embedded",len(syms),flush=True); return syms,cache
overlap=lambda f,s,e,c: f==c["file"] and s<=c["span"][1] and e>=c["span"][0]
model=json.loads(urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request("http://localhost:11434/api/show",data=b'{"model":"nomic-embed-text"}',headers={"Content-Type":"application/json"})).read()).get("details",{})
idx={}; caches={}
for fx in sorted({c["fx"] for c in cases}): idx[fx],caches[fx]=index_for(fx)
qv=[norm(v) for v in embed([f"search_query: {c[field]}" for c in cases])]
rows=[]
for i,(c,q) in enumerate(zip(cases,qv)):
    g=json.load(open(f"{gdir}/{i:02d}.json")).get("results",[])
    prim=[x for x in g if not x.get("section") and x.get("rank") and x["rank"]<=10]
    grank=next((x["rank"] for x in prim if overlap(x["file_path"],x.get("symbol_start_line") or x["start_line"],x.get("symbol_end_line") or x["end_line"],c)),None)
    top=sorted(idx[c["fx"]],key=lambda x:-sum(a*b for a,b in zip(q,x["v"])))[:10]
    erank=next((k+1 for k,x in enumerate(top) if overlap(x["file"],x["s"],x["e"],c)),None)
    rows.append({"i":i,"graph_rank":grank,"embed_rank":erank,"graph_primary_rows":len(prim)})
summ=lambda key:(lambda ok:{"found10":len(ok),"top3":sum(r<=3 for r in ok),"rank1":sum(r==1 for r in ok)})([r[key] for r in rows if r[key]])
out={"label":label,"cases":cases_path,"cases_sha":sha(cases_path),"field":field,"graph_dir":gdir,
     "graph_binary_note":open(f"{gdir}/BINARY").read().strip() if os.path.exists(f"{gdir}/BINARY") else "UNRECORDED (pre-control run)",
     "model":"nomic-embed-text","model_details":model,"embed_cache_sha":{k:sha(v) for k,v in caches.items()},
     "graph":summ("graph_rank"),"embedding":summ("embed_rank"),
     "paired_embed_better":sum(1 for r in rows if (r["embed_rank"] or 99)<(r["graph_rank"] or 99)),
     "paired_graph_better":sum(1 for r in rows if (r["graph_rank"] or 99)<(r["embed_rank"] or 99)),"rows":rows}
json.dump(out,open(f"{S}/embed/fair-{label}.json","w"),indent=1)
print(label,"graph",out["graph"],"| embedding",out["embedding"],"| paired embed-better",out["paired_embed_better"],"graph-better",out["paired_graph_better"])
PY

## Setup

## Feature: an OPT-IN semantic retrieval channel for `query`/`search`
Evidence driving this (offline, exposed-DEV only): for realistic agent-phrased queries, local embeddings of function symbols found targets far more often than lexical BM25 (graph 14/40 vs 36/40 found@10). The frozen fusion rule is INTERLEAVE, EMBEDDING-FIRST, with canonical dedupe. Controls: verbatim doc queries and exact identifier queries were not harmed (graph rank-1 kept at position <= 2).

HARD requirements:
1. Opt-in ONLY. Default behaviour must be byte-identical when not configured. It is enabled only when BOTH env vars are set: ENTIRE_GRAPH_SEMANTIC_ENDPOINT (an Ollama-compatible base URL such as http://localhost:11434, whose POST /api/embed takes {"model","input":[...]} and returns {"embeddings":[[...]]}) and ENTIRE_GRAPH_SEMANTIC_MODEL. Also allow a CLI flag to turn it off per call if one is easy. Find where search options and env are plumbed (internal/cli search flags and EntireEnv; internal/sem SearchOptions) and follow that pattern.
2. Index build. A subcommand or flag on the existing index/preindex path (find the existing `index` command and PreindexProviderSnapshot) builds a semantic index for a COMMITTED tree only (never worktree mode; the existing cache refuses worktree modes for policy reasons, so respect that). Contents: for every function/method symbol, text = "search_document: <split name words>. <doc comment> <signature line>" (reuse existing doc/signature extraction if present, otherwise the leading comment block plus the declaration line), truncated to about 1500 chars, embedded in batches, L2-normalised float32. Store it beside the snapshot cache, keyed by tree + model name + text-recipe version constant + embedding dimension. Write atomically (unique temp plus rename). Validate cardinality and dimension on load; any mismatch means the index is unusable and falls back.
3. Query time. If enabled AND a valid index exists for the current tree/model/recipe AND the search is not in worktree mode:
   - embed "search_query: <query>" with a short timeout (e.g. 3s);
   - cosine top-K (K=10) over the index;
   - NOMINATE those symbols' files into the file selection BEFORE the MaxIndexedFiles cut (a separate small budget of the K files, disclosed in stats), so their symbols can be rendered;
   - after lexical ranking, FUSE the primary results (not related/covering-test sections) by interleave E-first: e1, g1, e2, g2, ..., dedupe by (file, symbol start line), cut to the requested top-k, and re-number ranks.
   Keep sections and auxiliaries logic otherwise unchanged.
4. FAIL-OPEN. Endpoint down, timeout, HTTP error, model mismatch, a missing or invalid index, or a dimension mismatch all fall back to pure lexical output. Add a stats/diagnostic field (e.g. SemanticStatus: off|used|unavailable:<reason>) and no crash. When enabled but unavailable, add a single warning line, following how existing warnings are surfaced.
5. No new external Go dependencies (use net/http, encoding/json, math).

## Tests (fake server via httptest; deterministic vectors keyed by text, e.g. hash words into 8-16 dims)
- Default-off: with the env vars unset, output is identical to baseline, compared as JSON bytes on a fixture.
- Nomination: a fixture where lexical search does NOT retrieve the target, the fake embedding makes the target the nearest neighbour, and with the channel enabled the target appears at rank 1 (interleave E-first).
- Lexical rank-1 preserved at position <= 2 under the channel.
- Fail-open: server returns 500 / hangs past the timeout / wrong dimension: output equals lexical, SemanticStatus reports unavailable, no panic.
- Index is keyed by tree: after a new commit (changed tree) the old index is not used.
- Worktree mode never uses the channel.
- Atomic write: no temp residue after a build.
Prove each guard by a mutation (drop the tree key, drop the fallback, drop the dedupe, drop the E-first order) that turns its test RED, and record it.

Commit(s) on feat/semantic-channel, with no push. Report:
- files changed and design choices, especially where nomination hooks into selection and how the budget is disclosed;
- test list and results;
- the mutation table;
- the command to build the index and the env vars;
- known limits.

# FRESH semantic-channel evaluation — pre-registration
Written 2026-09-28 BEFORE any case was selected, any query written, or any arm run on this repository.
The fusion rule (interleave, embedding-first, dedupe by file+symbol start) was FROZEN earlier on DEV data and is not changed here.

## Population
- Repository: entire-brain, cloned to scratchpad/fx-brain at a pinned commit (recorded in cases.json). Never used before in
  the locate, paraphrase or semantic work.
- 40 targets, Go function/method symbols, name >= 6 chars, body >= 5 lines, selected with seed 29:
  20 WITH a doc comment (>= 10 words) and 20 WITHOUT any leading comment (to measure the doc-comment bias).
- Queries: one realistic agent-style query per target, written by a model from the function SOURCE (and doc, if any),
  under the same rules as dev_realistic (no 3+ word copy of the doc, no glued symbol name, 6-25 words), checked
  mechanically. A second, separate control query per target: the bare symbol name.

## Arms (same binary lineage, same flags: --profile full --format json --top-k 10, committed tree)
- B: the semantic-channel branch with the channel OFF (env unset) — lexical baseline, identical code.
- C: the same binary with the channel ON (local nomic-embed-text), index built for the pinned tree.
Primary comparison C vs B. Scoring = fair rule: primary rows only, rank <= 10, same file + symbol span overlaps target.

## Metrics
- Primary: found@10 on the realistic queries. Secondary: top3, rank1; paired Hit@10 wins/losses/ties; each reported
  separately for the documented and undocumented halves.
- Control: bare-name queries, found@10/top3/rank1 for B and C.

## Falsifier (any one fails the channel)
- C found@10 <= B found@10 on the realistic queries, OR
- C drops any case that B had in its top 3 out of the top 10 (realistic or control), OR
- control (bare-name) top3 for C falls more than 1 below B.
Paired Hit@10 significance: at n=40, >= 6 net discordant wins with no losses is the minimum exact two-sided p<=.05.

## Limits
Model-written queries; one repository; retrieval rank only (no task or token claim); requires a local embedding model.

The held-out test is running locally and nothing has been scored yet, so no result is in. It's slow: about 24 seconds per query. So far only 28 of the 240 queries have finished (all in B-realistic). It runs one query at a time at low priority, and I expect it to take around 1.5 hours.

What's running, on 40 new queries against the entire-brain repo:
- **B:** the new build with the semantic channel off.
- **C:** the same build with it on, using the local embedding model (index built for 11,993 symbols).
- **A:** the version from before the feature. It starts automatically once B and C finish.

**A slip I need to flag:** Codex had asked me to hold these runs until the exact setup was pinned down, and I read that message after I'd already started them. Nothing had been scored or opened, so the results aren't biased. Before scoring I wrote and hashed an addendum to the pre-registration that pins:
- both builds (the new branch and the pre-feature version, both clean)
- the model version and every flag, including the default 24 KiB output budget
- no retries: a failed query counts as a miss, and this set of queries can't be reused after this run

I told Codex all of this.

I also took Codex's point that "channel off" should behave exactly like the pre-feature version, and made it a gate. If B's results differ from A's on any of the 80 queries, the run is reported as invalid instead of scored. After that, the channel passes or fails on the pre-registered rules that were already frozen.

The branch stays unpublished until Codex's two code reviews come back. Separately, Codex published a new draft PR, #297, which fixes how results are counted; it passes 24/24 checks and only needs a reviewer's approval.

You haven't decided yet whether this tool may depend on a local embedding model, and Codex has asked you about it. I haven't treated your general "full authority" as that decision, and the channel is off unless it's explicitly configured.

I opened draft PR #298 for the search hang on `main`. The query that hung past the 300-second limit now finishes in about 37 seconds. The PR is not merged, and I reran its new tests myself and they pass.

**What it fixes**
- **The hang:** the search now hands `git grep` its patterns as one combined pattern instead of a dozen separate ones. That took the raw grep from over 60 seconds to 1.8. The rest of the 37 seconds is other work, not this bug.
- **Leftover processes:** stopping `entire-graph` normally (Ctrl-C or a regular kill) now also stops its `git grep`. A force-kill (`kill -9`) can still leave one running briefly, because macOS gives no way to prevent that. The PR says so.

**How it's checked**
- The new tests confirm the combined pattern returns exactly the same matches as the old code, on a test repo, across several kinds of pattern.
- Undoing each part of the fix makes a test fail.
- No stray `git grep` processes are left on your machine.

**Not fixed yet:** a second, case-insensitive search path has the same slowdown (28.6 seconds against 1.8). The same trick could change which characters count as matches, so I left it as a follow-up noted in the PR.

The fix round for the ten defects Codex found in the semantic branch is still running. The held-out test waits for it, and I'll record the exact fixed version in the pre-registration before any queries run. The question on whether to allow the optional local-model search is still open for you.

The semantic branch now has fixes for all ten defects Codex found. It's still unpublished, and the fresh test is waiting on Codex's second review.

**What I checked myself:**
- The new head (ca659afa) has no uncommitted changes, and Codex's six test files are byte-for-byte unchanged.
- Those tests all failed on the old version for the reasons Codex gave, and they all pass now.
- The fix agent undid each fix in turn to confirm a test catches it; 25 of those 26 checks failed as they should. The exception is one backup safeguard for cancelled index builds: removing it alone breaks nothing, because an earlier check catches the same case.
- With the feature switched off, output is byte-for-byte the same as the pre-feature version across 32 test queries.

**What changed in behaviour:**
- It only talks to an embedding model on your own machine and refuses any other address.
- It never shows a made-up relevance score.
- It no longer ranks a test above the code that needs fixing.
- It stays within the existing limit on how many files a search reads.
- It says in every output format whether semantic search was used.

**Test builds ready:** I built two versions for the fresh test, both including the grep-hang fix from PR #298:
- one with the semantic feature
- one pre-feature version, the baseline it has to beat

A third addendum to the pre-registration records exactly which builds and settings will be used. Every run gets the same prebuilt index, so the earlier problem of comparing two changes at once can't recur.

**Decisions only you can make.** None of these are settled by the fixes; I recorded them without choosing:
- **The big one:** should entire-graph offer optional semantic search that depends on a local embedding model (Ollama)? Codex asked you the same question.
- **Turning it on:** it's switched on only by two environment variables, with no explicit opt-in step.
- **Model version:** it uses the `:latest` model tag rather than a pinned version, so results could shift when the model updates.
- **Small-limit case:** the top plain-search file is never displaced, so with a one-file limit the feature can't add anything.
- **Low confidence:** an answer made only of semantic matches is marked low-confidence.

I'm watching for Codex's reply and will launch the fresh test once it has no blocking objections.

  **N1, BLOCKING (eval fairness and correctness): on the warm exact-preindex path, nominations evict lexically matched files and change the lexical IDF.**
  - On the `git-tree-grep` path, every matched file is kept on purpose; the code comment at `search.go:2546` says MaxIndexedFiles is not a recall cap there. That makes `len(selected) > maxFiles`, so `free=0` and every nomination evicts a tail file (`search_semantic.go:303-319`).
  - The tail order is path-prior order (`committedSearchFiles`, `search.go:3437`), not content relevance. So the claim that "the lexical head is the best lexical evidence" does not hold on this path.
  - With `corpusFromSelected=true`, IDF DF is `selectedContentDF` over the selected files (`search.go:4073`). Evicted files carrying query terms therefore lower DF while N stays fixed, and the scores are still reported as exact.
  - Test `TestRereviewWarmPathLexicalCorpusUnchanged` (profile full, preindexed, MaxIndexedFiles 2):

**Retrieval checks out.** With the prebuilt index, switched-on search leaves the normal results, their word-rarity weighting and their order exactly as they are with it off. Nothing in the new code was wrong.

**Two display steps can hide a correct result from the scorer.** I'm handling them differently:

content.text:
**The pre-registered fresh test passed, but the verdict depends on a scoring change I made before the feature-on run.** Under the original rule it would have failed on one case.

This is the first held-out result for semantic search in entire-graph. It used a repository never touched before (entire-brain) and 40 targets, and those queries can't be reused now.

**Check that the feature changes nothing when it's off:** with the feature off, results were identical to the pre-feature version on all 80 queries. That covers files, lines, rank, score and signals. None of the 240 queries across the three arms errored, and semantic search actually ran on all 80 feature-on queries.

**Realistic, plain-language queries (40):**

| | Found in top 10 | Top 3 | Rank 1 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Feature off | 22 | 19 | 16 |
| Feature on | **29** | **24** | **19** |

- **Paired comparison:** the feature found 7 targets the plain search missed and lost none (33 unchanged). That's statistically significant (p = 0.016).
- **By half:** documented functions went from 12 to 16 found, and undocumented ones from 10 to 13.
- **Exact-name controls:** both arms found all 40 targets in the top 3. Rank-1 hits dropped slightly, 21 → 19, because a semantic match can now sit above an exact name match.

**Why it hinges on the scoring change:** under the original rule, which only counts a hit when the result's symbol overlaps the target, the numbers are 21 → 26 found, 6 wins and 1 loss. That loss was a case plain search had in its top 3, which trips the pre-registered failure rule.

In that case the target was merged into the feature's top result: the rank-1 row shows lines 4–46, which include the target's lines 40–46. So the agent is shown the target code; the old rule just doesn't count it. A reviewer predicted exactly this before the run. I then changed the rule to also count the lines actually displayed, and recorded and applied that change to all arms before any feature-on output existed. I'm reporting both readings; Codex has both, and I've asked it to challenge this point specifically.

**What this doesn't show:**
- It's one repo, with model-written queries.
- It measures whether the right code appears in the ranked results, not token savings or whether tasks succeed.
- It only covers searches that use the prebuilt index.
- Speed is about the same (median 37 vs 39 seconds per query, on a busy machine).

**Getting here took three fix rounds.** Each round introduced a new bug that only a fresh reviewer caught, not the passing tests. It also turned up a real hang on `main` that was burning your CPU, which is fixed in PR #298.

**Decisions only you can make:**
1. Should entire-graph offer semantic search that needs a local embedding model (Ollama)? It's off by default and only talks to your own machine. With a yes, I'll open the branch as a draft PR (no merge), with the open product questions listed.
2. The draft PRs waiting for review: #292 → #293 → #286 → #294 → #285, #297 and #298.

The full write-up is `scratchpad/fresh-run/FINDINGS.md`.

**DRAFT — do not merge.** An unresolved product decision blocks merge (see below). Stacked on #285 (`bench/locate-cost`, a10582ab).

## What
Adds an **opt-in** semantic retrieval channel to `entire graph query`. A local embedding model nominates files and symbols, and the results are fused embedding-first with the lexical ranking.
- **Off by default.** It turns on only when both `ENTIRE_GRAPH_SEMANTIC_ENDPOINT` and `ENTIRE_GRAPH_SEMANTIC_MODEL` are set. When unconfigured, output is byte-identical to the base across 32 queries × 4 formats × 3 env states.
- `entire graph index --semantic` builds the index. Queries use it only with `--head` (the committed tree); `--no-semantic` turns it off per call.
- **Loopback only:** `localhost` or a literal loopback IP. No proxy, no redirects, and names are never resolved by the dialer.
- **Fails open to lexical** with a `W_SEMANTIC_UNAVAILABLE` warning and a stable code, for a missing index, a timeout, a bad response or a failed nomination snapshot. The reported state is visible in text, agent and JSON output.
- **Lexical invariance, warm path:** nominations never change lexical scores, IDF or the candidate pool. This is tested against the pre-fusion ranking exactly.

## Evidence: fresh preregistered evaluation (population now spent)
The fixture repository had never been used in this work. It has 40 targets (20 documented, 20 not) and model-written realistic queries. The preregistration, three addenda, hashes and the per-query receipts are all written before the arms ran. Gate: channel OFF == pre-feature base on 80/80 queries (rows, spans, ranks, scores, signals).

| realistic, n=40 | found@10 | top3 | rank1 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| channel off | 22 | 19 | 16 |
| channel on (`nomic-embed-text`) | **29** | **24** | **19** |

- Paired wins/losses/ties: 7/0/33, exact sign test p = 0.016.
- Bare-name controls: top3 40/40 in both arms; rank1 21 → 19.
- **Scorer disclosure:** the verdict depends on a scorer rule fixed before any channel-on output existed. A hit counts if the target overlaps a row's symbol span **or its displayed span**. Under the original symbol-span-only rule the result is 21 → 26, W/L 6/1, and the one loss fails the "baseline top-3 lost" clause. That case is a same-file span merge that folds the target into the rank-1 row, whose displayed lines 4–46 include the target (40–46).
- **Limits:** one repository; model-written queries; retrieval rank only (no token, cost or task claim); warm preindexed path only.

## Review history
Two peer reviews (query and safety, Q1–Q5 and F1–F5) and two fresh adversarial re-reviews. Every round found real defects, including defects introduced by earlier fixes. Every finding has a RED→GREEN regression test, and every fix has verified-by-weakening mutation evidence.

## Blocking decisions (human)
1. **Should the product depend on a local model at all?** This is a trust and resources decision.
2. Activation/consent: currently env-only.
3. Model identity: the `:latest` alias is not pinned by digest.
4. Cold path: nominations evict lexical tail files under `--max-indexed-files`. That is disclosed in `semantic_evicted_files`, but it shifts the surviving BM25 scores slightly.
5. `semantic_results` now counts rows the channel matched; the JSON format version is not bumped.

Related: #298 (a `git grep` multi-pattern hang on `main`, found during this evaluation).

- **CI:** all 28 checks pass on Linux, macOS and Windows, covering build, lint and the full test suites.
- **Entire Gates:** automated checks pass, the agent review found no blocking issues, and the branch is up to date. The only failure is **Approvals**, because no reviewer has approved it yet.

It stays a draft that I won't merge. Before it could merge, you'd need to decide whether entire-graph should depend on a local embedding model.

**Still running:** an agent is fixing the remaining slow text search (the case-insensitive exact-text path). That fix will be added to PR #298.

**Waiting on you:**
1. The local-model decision for #300.
2. Approvals for the other draft PRs: #292 → #293 → #286 → #294 → #285, #297 and #298.

I went with none of options (a), (b) or (c): they are not equivalent, and the fix is a PCRE2 alternation instead. Commit `ae9c03f1` sits on top of b7cba987 and is pushed. Draft PR #298 now points at it; I posted a comment (https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph/pull/298#issuecomment-5886218354) and also replaced the PR body's "Limits" bullet, which said this path was not fixed.
  
  **Why the earlier worry was wrong.** git v2.54.0 grep.c no longer uses kwset. In a git built with PCRE2, `-F -i` goes through `compile_pcre2_pattern` with CASELESS, plus UTF|UCP under a UTF-8 locale. A `-P -i` pattern goes through the same function with the same options. Measured under en_US.UTF-8, on both /opt/homebrew/bin/git 2.54.0 and Apple /usr/bin/git 2.50.1 (both have PCRE2):
  - `k` matches the Kelvin sign.
  - `s` matches ſ, as in `databaſe`.
  - σ matches Σ and ς.
  - μ matches µ.
  - `i` does not match İ or ı, and `ß` does not match `ss`.
  
  Option (a) (ASCII-folded ERE) and an `-E -i` alternation both miss the Kelvin sign and ſ under UTF-8, so neither is equivalent. All modes agree under LC_ALL=C. (b) cannot rebuild git's combined match chain or its per-file `-m` count. (c) would still run the slow multi-pattern grep on the big file. Receipt: `fold-probe.txt`.
  
  **The fix.** `-F -i -e w1 -e w2 …` becomes one `-P -i -e '\Qw\E|…'`, with the longest words first.
  - **Match choice:** for `-o`, git's `match_next_pattern` takes the leftmost match across patterns, and the longest when two start at the same place. PCRE2 takes the first branch that matches at the leftmost start. Case-insensitive PCRE2 matches one character per pattern character, so two words matching at one spot are a word and its extension. Sorting longest first therefore picks the same match.
  - **Rest of the command:** which lines match and how `-m` counts them follow from this, and every other flag is unchanged.
  - **Plain vs `\Q…\E` form:** words without git's regex specials are compiled as-is, which PCRE2 treats as literal, so the `\Q…\E` form matches the same.
  
  **Timings.** Both columns go through pgrun on fx-brain @4623fab, git 2.54.0, and every row gave identical `[]GrepMatch`:
  
  | input | tree | old | new |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | 13 words | worktree | 39.95s | 0.08s |
  | 13 words | HEAD | 53.80s | 0.22s |
  | 6 words | worktree | 3.15s | 0.11s |

  | raw git, 13 words | worktree | 30.2–37.8s | 0.13s |
  
  The raw git outputs are byte-identical (5,258,385 B each).
  
  I could not reproduce the old end-to-end query slowdown. My end-to-end `search` runs never reached this code: on a clean worktree (and on the dirty local clone I made) no `-o` call showed up in the git call log, and old and new binaries both took about 27s. So the gain is shown at the function level and in raw git, not through the CLI.
  
  **Tests added**, in `internal/gitutil/grep_fixed_alternation_test.go`:
  - **Shape:** `TestGrepFixedStringAlternationShape` checks the exact pattern string for ordering, dedup, metacharacters, and each input that must fall back.
  - **Equivalence:** `TestGrepFixedStringMatchesAlternationMatchesLegacyMultiPattern` compares against the old raw git call on a stress fixture.
    - Cases: words that are prefixes of others, overlapping and adjacent matches, metacharacters.
    - Characters: Kelvin sign, ſ, İ/ı, ß, Greek.
    - Combinations: 60 subtests (C and UTF-8 locales × 5 pattern sets × `-m 1/3/32` × worktree/HEAD).
    - It fails if the UTF-8 run never folds a non-ASCII character.
  - **Call check:** `TestGrepFixedStringMatchesSendsOneAlternation` logs the actual arguments sent to git.
  - **Fallback:** `REDACTED` checks the fallback for a git built without PCRE2.
  - **Related suites:** the gitutil grep tests and the related sem preselection tests pass.
  
  **Mutations** (every one turned the tests red):
  
  | mutation | failing tests |
  |---|---|
  | Full revert of git.go to b7cba987 | build fails, test helpers undefined |
  | Call site bypassed (old `-F` command always) | SendsOneAlternation |
  | Longest-first sort removed | Shape, Equivalence, SendsOne |
  | Option (a), ASCII-folded ERE | Equivalence: 12 subtests, all UTF-8, none in C |
  | `-E -i` alternation | Equivalence: the same 12 UTF-8 subtests |
  | Non-ASCII patterns accepted | Shape |
  | Backslash accepted | Shape |
  | Missing-PCRE2 detection removed | FallsBack |
  
  The (a) and `-E -i` runs also turned SendsOne and FallsBack red, but only as a side effect of the mutation dropping `-P`.
  
  **Inputs that still use the old `-F` command:**
  - Non-ASCII patterns: git builds locale-based folding tables for those.
  - Patterns containing a backslash (a `\E` would end the quoting early) or a newline (git splits `-e` patterns on it).
  - git built without PCRE2: it would compile `-F` with the platform regex instead. This is caught from git's exit 128 with "not compiled with USE_LIBPCRE".

The second slow-search fix is on draft PR #298: case-insensitive whole-word matching dropped from 40–54 seconds to under a quarter of a second (13 words: 39.95s → 0.08s on the working tree, 53.8s → 0.22s on HEAD). It returns exactly the same matches as before.

I checked the main compatibility claim myself on a small test file:

| Search | Matches |
|---|---|
| Old (`-F -i -e k -e s`) | `K K ſ k` |
| New (`-P -i 'k\|s'`) | `K K ſ k` (identical) |

- **When it falls back:** the old command still runs when a word has non-ASCII letters, contains a backslash or newline, or git lacks the regex library the fix needs.
- **Limit:** the agent couldn't get an end-to-end `entire graph` search to reach this code, so the speedup is shown on the function and raw git, not on a full search.

PR #298 (the grep-hang fix) is now held up only by reviewer approval. The automated review had flagged two problems as blocking; I tested both and neither is a real bug.

- **High, "backslash inside `[...]` breaks the combined pattern":** in git's regex syntax a backslash inside brackets is just an ordinary character. - **Medium, "goroutine leak":** it isn't one. Go's documentation says the deferred `stop()` cancels the context, which lets the goroutine exit. In a check, 100 calls left 2 goroutines, not 101; one of the two is Go's own signal watcher.

The CLI command for dismissing findings returns a 404, so I posted both refutations with the evidence as a comment on #298. The medium one may still show as open until someone dismisses it in the web interface.

The token-cost study is now running, and nothing has been scored yet. It runs one query at a time at low priority, and each finished group of queries will show up here.

What I checked before approving it:
- **Frozen files:** all 9 files match their recorded hashes.
- **Queries:** all 40 pass the mechanical check that they don't copy the target's documentation or name. I read six by hand, and they describe what the code does rather than giving the answer away.
- **Test repo:** it has no uncommitted changes. It's `entirehq/mcp`, because every other candidate had already been tested or had a flaw.
- **Pinned tools:** the search binary and the embedding model version are pinned, and the run stops if the model version differs.

The setup compares three approaches at 2, 4 and 8 KiB, on 40 realistic queries plus 40 exact-name controls:
- **G:** a strong grep strategy designed to give grep its best shot.
- **L:** graph search.
- **E:** graph search with semantic search.

A query counts as found only if the function's declaration line actually appears in the output. That rule leans against the graph; I kept it anyway, because a conservative rule is the honest choice. Two validity checks run after the arms:
- the semantic arm's index, with semantic search switched off, must give the same results as plain graph search;
- semantic search must have been active on at least 36 of 40 queries.

**What counts as success, fixed in advance:**
- Semantic search finds at least 4 more of the 40 targets than plain graph search.
- The difference is statistically significant (p ≤ 0.05).
- Grep does not beat it.
- It doesn't cost more bytes to reach the target.

The main limits are also written down in advance. It's a small repo, which helps grep. It measures only the first call; a real agent would search again. And half the targets are test functions.

Decisions still waiting on you:
1. Should entire-graph offer semantic search that runs a local embedding model? This decides whether #300 can ever merge.
2. Approvals on PRs #292 → #293 → #286 → #294 → #285, #297, #298 and #300.

content.text:
**Study 3 ran cleanly, and semantic search failed its pre-registered test.** At the same byte budget, it didn't show an agent the target code any more often than plain graph search. Graph search did beat a strong grep on descriptive queries, and grep was cheaper for exact-name lookups.

**Setup**
- **Repo:** `entireio/git-sync`, never used in any earlier study.
- **Targets:** 40, each tried at 2, 4 and 8 KiB, 880 calls in all with 0 failures.
- **Validity checks, both passed on all 80 checked queries:**
  - with semantic search switched off, its index gave output byte-for-byte identical to plain graph search, with the timing line masked;
  - with it switched on, semantic search actually ran.
- **What counts as found:** the target's declaration line appears in one call's output.

**Targets found, out of 40 realistic queries:**

| | 2 KiB | 4 KiB | 8 KiB |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Grep, phrase-first | 9 | 13 | 15 |
| Graph search | 17 | 21 | 22 |
| Graph search with semantic | 18 | 21 | 24 |

**What it shows**
- **Semantic search: no gain at equal budget.** At 4 KiB it tied plain graph search, 21 to 21, winning 4 queries and losing 4. That meets the pre-registered failure condition. The earlier study's win was about ranking: the target moved into the top 10 with no size limit. Here, a better rank didn't mean the agent saw more target code, because the rows above the target used up the budget.
- **Graph search beats grep on descriptive queries.** The direction holds at every budget (21 vs 13 at 4 KiB). With 40 queries the study is underpowered, though: only 2 of the comparisons reach p ≤ 0.05, and the 4 KiB one doesn't. Grep didn't find the target within 8 KiB for 25 of 40 queries; graph search's median cost to find it was about 3.9 KB.
- **Grep wins exact-name lookups.** Every approach found all 40 at 4 KiB, but grep needed a median 666 bytes against about 1,850 for graph search, roughly 2.8× cheaper.

What I did with the results:
- posted the negative result on #300 and narrowed its claim to "better ranking only";
- sent the numbers to Codex;
- wrote `scratchpad/fresh3/FINDINGS.md`;
- recorded both lessons in memory.

**Caveats:** one repo; one person wrote all the queries; only the first call is measured; the "declaration line shown" rule is strict and leans against graph search. The build tested also includes a merge I resolved by hand; it isn't in any PR and hasn't been reviewed.

**Where this leaves the product:** the case I can defend is that graph search finds code from a description better than grep does, at the same output size. Getting past "underpowered" needs more studies like this one: new repos, no new features. #300 has no claim beyond ranking, so I'd lean toward not merging it.

**Waiting on you:**
1. Whether to keep #300 at all.
2. Approvals for #292 → #293 → #286 → #294 → #285, #297, #298 and #301.

content.text:
**Study 4 is valid. Graph search beat grep, but the result is not statistically significant, so the pre-registered success test was not met.**

- **Setup:** 80 descriptive queries across two repos no earlier study had used, comparing graph search on `main` plus the two fixes against a strong grep strategy.
- **Validity:** all 490 calls completed with no failures, repeat runs gave identical output, and every call used the pinned binary.

**Pre-registered primary result (4 KiB budget):**
- Graph search showed the target's declaration line for 38 of 80 queries; grep for 29.
- Graph won 20 of the queries where they disagreed and grep won 11, which gives p = 0.15.
- That clears the required margin (graph ahead by at least 8) but misses significance, so success is **not met**. The failure test (graph no better than grep) did **not** fire.
- The pre-registration warned of this: the study had only about a 68% chance of reaching significance even if graph search really is better.

**The direction is the same everywhere else:**

| Budget | Grep | Graph | Graph wins / grep wins | p |
|---|--:|--:|---|--:|
| 2 KiB | 16 | 28 | 19 / 7 | 0.029 |
| 4 KiB | 29 | 38 | 20 / 11 | 0.15 |
| 8 KiB | 38 | 45 | 17 / 10 | 0.25 |

- Graph search is at least even with grep in every subgroup: both repos, documented and undocumented code, and source and test files.
- **It also returns fewer bytes.** At 8 KiB it returned about 43% fewer bytes in total (374k vs 653k) while finding more targets. Part of that gap is by design, because the grep strategy always fills its budget.
- Adding in study 3 gives graph 34 wins to grep's 17, p = 0.024. I combined them after seeing the results, so treat that as exploratory, not a pre-registered result.

**The defensible claim today:** graph search consistently finds described code better than a strong grep at the same output size, while returning fewer bytes. No single pre-registered test has yet cleared p ≤ 0.05 at the primary budget. Settling it needs about 150 more fresh queries; reusing old ones wouldn't count. Codex has the numbers, and the write-up is in `scratchpad/fresh4/FINDINGS.md`.

I opened draft PR #302, which makes exact-name lookups (a query that is just a symbol's name) much cheaper. It isn't ready yet: a second review is still running.

**What it changes:** when the query exactly matches a symbol's name (case-sensitive), graph search shows only that symbol's definition, or all of them if several share the name. It also adds a line saying other results were left out. If that compact answer doesn't fit the output limit, the output is exactly what it was before.

**Before and after, on 30 name lookups in the entire-graph repo** (a repo no study used for these tests):

| Output limit | Definition found, before → after | Median bytes, before → after |

| 1 KiB | 1 → 27 | 846 → 995 |
| 2 KiB | 19 → 27 | 1,854 → 1,486 |
| 4 KiB | 27 → 27 | 3,440 → 1,486 |
| Default (24 KiB) | 27 → 27 | 6,093 → 1,486 (−76%) |

- It never shows fewer definitions than before, and no output goes over its limit.
- The 3 names it misses sit inside test strings and aren't real definitions, so the old version missed them too.
- For queries that aren't exact names, output stays byte-identical, and a test checks that.
- The agent also found why study 3 missed exact names at 2 KiB: the limit was split evenly across all 10 results, so the matching result got about 170 bytes and no room for its code.

- names with many definitions
- declarations spanning several lines
- whether dropping the "how to verify" section at tight limits leaves the agent worse off
- whether the 30 test names were a biased sample

PR #302 (compact exact-name lookups) isn't ready: an independent review found a blocking bug, and I reproduced it myself.

**The blocking bug:** in Java and C#, the index records a function as starting on its annotation line (`@Override`, `[Obsolete]`), not on its signature. At tight budgets the compact answer shows only that annotation line. With the reviewer's test, 74 budget sizes lose the signature line that the old output showed. That breaks the PR's core promise that it never finds less than before. Our tests and measurements were Go-only, so they missed it.

**Smaller problems it also found:**
- **Validation instructions dropped:** at tight budgets (around 400–480 bytes), the answer can drop the instructions on how to validate the change, against the tool's own rule.
- **Replayed searches:** when a session only allows one search, later searches get the truncated exact-name answer back. Its advice to "search a phrase" instead then leads nowhere.
- **Silent truncation:** if a name has many definitions, say 46 `Error`s, and all ten slots are exact matches, the answer shows 9 with no hint that more exist.
- **Doc comments:** the compact answer drops them.
- **Overstated measurement:** the before/after table was Go-only and included easy names, so it claimed more than it showed.

What held up:
- Queries that aren't exact names produce byte-identical output to before.
- JSON and text output are unchanged.
- Common names like `Run`, `Handler` or `Error` didn't trigger the mode on the fixture.
- Unusual inputs (unicode, dotted names like `pkg.Func`) fall back to normal search.
- Output never exceeds the size limit.

content.text:
**Study 5 met its pre-registered success test: graph search beat a strong grep.** This is the first significant pre-registered result for the core claim.

- **Setup:** 200 plain-English "find this code" queries across 5 repos not used in earlier studies. Three belong to the org; two are open-source repos at release tags.
- **Build tested:** the shippable version, `main` plus #298, #301 and #302.
- **Validity:** every validity check passed. All 1,220 runs used the pinned build, repeat runs gave identical output, and the frozen study files were unchanged afterwards.

**The pre-registered result:** with each tool limited to 4 KiB of output from a single call, graph search showed the target's declaration for **79 of 200** queries. Grep showed it for **52**. Graph search won 56 of the queries where the two disagreed and grep won 29, **p = 0.0045**. It also returned fewer bytes: a median of 3,340 vs 4,070 bytes.

**Weak spots:**
- **Other output sizes:** at 2 KiB (49 vs 40) and 8 KiB (91 vs 77), graph search is ahead but not significantly.
- **Undocumented code at 2 KiB:** grep did better, 20 vs 15.
- **Not every repo:** there are big wins on two repos (entire-search 17 vs 6, urfave/cli 19 vs 9) and near-ties on the other three.
- **Even the winner misses often:** graph search shows the target in one call only 40% of the time.

**What this lets us claim, word for word:** *"On descriptive locate queries at an equal 4 KiB budget, entire-graph shows the target declaration significantly more often than a strong grep (79 vs 52 of 200, p = 0.0045, pre-registered, 5 fresh repos), while returning fewer bytes."*

It does **not** support claims about task success, end-to-end token savings, other output sizes, or every repo winning.

Combining all three studies after the fact gives 90 wins to 46 (p = 0.0002). That's exploratory, not pre-registered. The write-up is in `scratchpad/fresh5/FINDINGS.md`, and Codex has it.

**What's left before launch needs you:**
1. **Merge approvals** for the draft PRs: #292 → #293 → #286 → #294 → #285, #297, #298 (grep hang), #301 (output changing with timing) and #302 (exact-name lookups). Their CI is green.
2. **Semantic search (#300):** improved ranking, but no gain at equal budget. My recommendation is not to merge it.

2. an "N lines elided" note,

**#303 isn't ready.** The independent review found a real bug, and I reproduced it myself. Separately, the machine was badly overloaded, which I've fixed.

**The review of #303 (always show the declaration line):**
- **Blocking bug:** when a decorator or annotation contains the function's own name, such as `@Named("fooBar")` or `@app.route("/login")`, that line is taken as the declaration. The output can then hide the real signature. In the reviewer's test this happened at 49 different output sizes. The same logic is in #302, so both need fixing.
- **A wrong claim in the PR:** it says each added declaration line costs at most one body line. It can cost three, because the "N lines elided" markers weren't being counted.
- **Misleading line numbers:** in most shortened blocks the header gives the line that matched the query, but the first line printed is the declaration, several lines earlier. An agent could read the wrong line number from that.
- **What held up:** output never exceeds its size limit (3,000 randomised runs), results don't depend on timing, and there's no new slowdown. On a sample chosen at random rather than one favouring the fix, it still helped: at 4 KiB the target's declaration was shown for 17 of 22 queries instead of 8.

**The CPU problem:** the machine's load average was 137. The reviewer's leftover test runs were still going, about a dozen `git grep` processes at around 130% CPU each, some for over an hour. Branches #301 → #302 → #303 were built from `main` without #298, so they still have the grep hang that #298 fixes. I killed all of them, stopped the reviewer, and the load is falling. Any binary used for measuring now has to include #298, every run goes through a wrapper that kills leftover child processes, and I've saved that rule to memory.

**Now running:** a fix agent is making these changes, with the new rules applied:
- #302: the declaration finder now skips decorators, annotations and string contents.
- #303: rebuilt on top of the fixed #302, with the reviewer's tests adopted, the accounting claim corrected, and the declaration's line number shown in the header.
- Re-measuring on both the original sample and a randomly chosen one.

**Waiting on you:**
1. Approvals for #292 → #293 → #286 → #294 → #285, #297, #298 and #301. #302 will need approval once its fix lands.
2. Whether to keep #300. I recommend not merging it.

**Status: the goal is not met, and I'd call the product not launch-ready.** The core claim has now passed a proper pre-registered test. What blocks launch is your approvals, plus two fixes still in progress.

**What's proven** (study 5: pre-registered, 200 queries, 5 fresh repos):
- When an agent searches in plain English with a 4 KiB output limit, graph search showed the right function's declaration **79 times vs 52 for a strong grep** (p = 0.0045), and it used fewer bytes.
- **Limits of that result:**
  - At 2 KiB and 8 KiB, graph search was ahead but not by a significant margin.
  - On 3 of the 5 repos it was a near-tie.
  - Graph search still misses the target 60% of the time on the first call.
- Nothing yet shows it helps agents finish tasks or saves tokens over a whole session.

**Bugs fixed along the way, each as a draft PR with CI green:**
- **#298:** a `git grep` hang that burned CPU for minutes per query.
- **#301:** output that changed depending on how long a query took.
- **#302:** exact-name lookups returned too much output. At 4 KiB the median answer shrank from 2,735 to 996 bytes, and nothing that was found before is now missed.

**In progress now:**
- **#303**, always showing the declaration line. This addresses the biggest cause of misses: 40 of the 121 in study 5.
  - A review found a bug: a decorator that contains the function's name, like `@app.route("/login")`, gets mistaken for the declaration.
  - A fix agent has already committed the corrected declaration-finder on #302. It is partway through the #303 fixes, with 3 regression-test commits so far, and is now running the full test suites.
  - In early measurements it raised declaration-found from 11 to 30 of 44 queries at 4 KiB. That's a sample I picked myself, so it isn't a claim yet.
- **Machine health:** load is down from 137 to about 30, and no runaway processes are left.

**Negative results, reported openly:**
- **Semantic search (#300)** improves ranking, but gave no gain at the same output budget (21 vs 21). My recommendation is not to merge it.
- **Two earlier studies:** study 2 was invalidated by the timing bug and never scored. Study 4 pointed the right way but wasn't statistically significant.

**What's left before a launch:**
1. **You:** approvals for #292 → #293 → #286 → #294 → #285, #297, #298 and #301, and once their fixes land, #302 and #303. Also a decision on #300.
2. **Me:** finish #303, get a fresh review of it, then run a new pre-registered study on fresh repos to confirm the declaration fix outside the data it came from.
3. **Not started, and I'd suggest it:** an end-to-end test of whether agents actually finish tasks faster or with fewer tokens. That is the claim a "100M-view" launch would need, and this campaign hasn't earned it yet.
